Utpiñjala, samutpiñja, and piñjala denote one who is greatly disturbed or confused.
For one of great aspiration there are udbhaṭa, udāra, udātta, udīrṇa, and mahāśaya.
Mahāmanas and mahātmā are also such terms; kṛpaṇa means a miser, mitaṃpaca.
Kīnāśa, taddhana, kṣudra, kadarya, and dṛḍhamuṣṭi denote that miser.
Kiṃpacāna is another such term; dayālu, kṛpālu, and karuṇāpara denote a compassionate person.

children.text: sūrato 'tha dayā śūkaḥ kāruṇyaṃ karuṇā ghṛṇā
children.translated_text: Sūrata means kindly disposed; dayā, śūka, kāruṇya, karuṇā, and ghṛṇā denote compassion.
Kṛpā, anukampā, and anukrośa also mean compassion; hiṃsra, śarāru, and ghātuka mean violent or destructive.

children.text: vyāpādanaṃ viśaraṇaṃ pramayaḥ pramāpaṇaṃ nigranthanaṃ pramathanaṃ kadanaṃ nibarhaṇam
children.translated_text: Vyāpādana, viśaraṇa, pramaya, pramāpaṇa, nigranthana, pramathana, kadana, and nibarhaṇa are terms for killing or destruction.

children.text: nisūdanaṃ viśasanaṃ kṣaṇanaṃ parāsanaṃ projjāsanaṃ praśamanaṃ pranighātanaṃ vadhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nisūdana, viśasana, kṣaṇana, parāsana, projjāsana, praśamana, pranighātana, and vadha likewise mean slaying or putting to death.
Pravāsana, udvāsana, ghāta, nirvāsana, saṃjñapti, niśumbha, and hiṃsā are words for expulsion, striking, or harm.
Nirvāpaṇa, ālambha, nisūdana, niryātana, unmantha, and samāpana are further terms for killing or bringing to an end.
Apāsana, varjana, mārapiñjā, niṣkāraṇa, ākrātha, and viśāraṇa denote removal, rejection, or destructive cutting off.

children.text: syuḥ kartane kalpanavardhane ca cchedaśca ghātodyata ātatāpī ||
children.translated_text: These are used for cutting, severing, and striking; cheda is cutting, and one intent on killing is ghātodyata or ātatāpī.
Saśīrṣacchedika and śīrṣacchedya describe one who deserves decapitation, that is, one worthy of execution.
Pramīta, upasaṃpanna, pareta, preta, and saṃsthita mean dead or departed.
One of whom only name, portrait, or fame remains is so described; vyāpanna and apagata also mean deceased or gone.
Parāsu means lifeless; a gift made on that day or for the deceased is called ūrdhvadehika.
Mṛtasnāna and apasnāna denote the bathing connected with a corpse; nivāpa is the offering of water or food to the ancestors.
Citi, cityā, and citā are equivalent terms for a funeral pyre; ṛju, prāñjala, and añjasa mean straight or upright.
Dakṣiṇa, sarala, and udāra mean honest or straightforward; śaṭha, nikuṭa, and anṛju mean crooked or deceitful.
Krūra, nṛśaṃsa, nistriṃśa, and pāpa mean cruel; dhūrta is vañcaka, a cheat.
Vyaṃsaka, kuhaka, dāṇḍājinika, māyin, and jālika are terms for deceivers or tricksters.

children.text: māyā tu śaṭhatā śāṭyaṃ kusṛtirniṣkṛtiśca sā ||
children.translated_text: Māyā is deceit: śaṭhatā, śāṭya, kusṛti, and niṣkṛti are its names.
Kapaṭa, kaitava, dambha, kūṭa, chadma, upadhi, and chala all denote fraud or deception.

children.text: vyapadeśo miṣaṃ lakṣaṃ nibhaṃ vyājo 'tha kukkuṭiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Vyapadeśa, miṣa, lakṣa, nibha, and vyāja mean a pretext or excuse; next comes kukkuṭi.

children.text: kuhanā dambhacaryā ca vañcanaṃ tu pratāraṇam
children.translated_text: Kukkuṭi, kuhanā, and dambhacaryā mean hypocrisy; vañcana is pratāraṇa, cheating.
Vyalīka and atisādhana denote false dealing; for a good person the terms are sādhu, sabhya, ārya, and sajjana.
Doṣaikadṛk and parobhāgī mean one who sees only faults; karṇejapa is a malicious whisperer or bad man.

children.text: piśunaḥ sūcako nīco dvijihvo matsarī khalaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Piśuna, sūcaka, nīca, dvijihva, matsarī, and khala are terms for a slanderous, base, or malicious person.
Vyasanārta means afflicted by vice or misfortune, and uparakta means affected or attached; a cora, a thief, is called pratirodhaka.
Dasyu, pāṭaccara, stena, taskara, and pāripanthika are names for thieves or robbers.
Parimoṣin, parāskandya, ekāgārika, and malimluca are further terms for thieves.

children.text: yaḥ paśyato haredarthaṃ sa cauraḥ paśyatoharaḥ ||
children.translated_text: One who takes property while the owner is looking is the thief called paśyatohara, 'one who steals in sight.'

children.text: cauryaṃ tu caurikā steyaṃ loptraṃ tvapahṛtaṃ dhanam
children.translated_text: Caurya, caurikā, and steya mean theft; loptra is stolen wealth.
Yadbhaviṣya and daivapara describe one who relies on fate; ālasya, śītaka, and alasa mean laziness or a lazy person.
Manda, tundaparimṛja, and anuṣṇa mean sluggish or idle; dakṣa is peśala, skillful.
Paṭu, uṣṇa, uṣṇaka, sūtthāna, catura, and tatpara mean able, energetic, clever, or intent on a task.
Āsakta, pravaṇa, prahva, prasita, and parāyaṇa mean attached, inclined, or devoted.
Dātṛ, udāra, sthūlalakṣa, and dānaśauṇḍa describe one who gives much or is generous.
Dāna, utsarjana, tyāga, pradeśana, and visarjana mean giving, relinquishing, or donation.
Vihāpita, vitaraṇa, sparśana, and pratipādana also denote distribution or bestowal.
Viśrāṇana, nirvapaṇa, apavarjana, and aṃhati are further words for giving or setting aside.
Arthavyayajña and sukala describe one who spends wealth in sacrifice or giving; a yācaka, a petitioner, is a vanīpaka.
Mārgaṇa, arthin, yācanaka, and tarkuka mean a beggar or seeker; arthanā and eṣaṇā denote seeking.
Ardanā, praṇaya, yācñā, yācanā, adhyeṣaṇā, and sani are terms for request or solicitation.
Utpatiṣṇu means rising or springing up; alaṃkariṣṇu and maṇḍana mean an adorner.
Bhaviṣṇu, bhavitṛ, and bhūṣṇu mean becoming or thriving; vartiṣṇu and vartana are equivalent terms for abiding or continuing.
Visṛtvara, visṛmara, prasārin, and visārin mean spreading or diffusive.
Lajjāśīla and apatrapiṣṇu mean bashful; sahiṣṇu, kṣamitṛ, and kṣamī mean patient or forbearing.

children.text: titikṣuḥ sahanaḥ kṣantā titikṣā sahanaṃ kṣamā
children.translated_text: Titikṣu, sahana, and kṣantṛ mean forbearing; titikṣā, sahana, and kṣamā mean forbearance or patience.
Īrṣyālu is jealous, and akṣānti and īrṣyā denote envy or intolerance; a krodhin, an angry person, is roṣaṇa.
Amarṣaṇa and krodhana also mean angry; caṇḍa means extremely irascible.
Bubhukṣita, kṣudhita, jighatsu, and aśanāyita mean hungry.
Bubhukṣā, aśanāyā, jighatsā, rocaka, and ruci denote hunger, appetite, or relish.
Pipāsu, tṛṣita, and tṛṣṇak mean thirsty; tṛṣṇā, tarṣa, and apalāsikā denote thirst.
Pipāsā, tṛṭ, tṛṣā, and udanyā are words for thirst; dhīti means drinking, and next comes śoṣaṇa.
Śoṣaṇa and rasādāna mean sucking up or taking in juice; a bhakṣaka, an eater, is ghasmara, admara, or āśitṛ.
Bhakta, anna, kūra, and andha mean food or cooked rice; bhitsā, dīdivi, and odana also denote boiled food.

children.text: aśanaṃ jīvanakaṃ ca yājo vājaḥ prasādanam ||
children.translated_text: Aśana, jīvanaka, yāja, vāja, and prasādana are terms for food or nourishment.
Bhissaṭā and dugdhikā denote milky or liquid food preparations; maṇḍa is here the chief essence of all flavors.
Mastu is the liquid from curds; from cooked rice come niḥsrāva, ācāma, and māsara.
Śrāṇā, vilepī, taralā, yavāgū, and uṣṇikā are names for gruel or thin cooked preparations.

children.text: sūpaḥ syātprahitaṃ sūdo vyañjanaṃ tu ghṛtādikam ||
children.translated_text: Sūpa is called prahita and sūda; vyañjana is a condiment or accompaniment such as ghee.
Kasuru and trisara are equivalent names for sesame-rice; next, piṣṭaka is described.
Piṣṭaka is pūpa or apūpa; pūlikā, polikā, pauli, and pūpikā are names for cakes.
For a slightly cooked cake the terms are abhyūṣa, abhyoṣa, and paulī.
Niṣṭhāna means temana, a moistening sauce; karambha is curds mixed with parched grain.
Ghṛtapūra, ghṛtavara, piṣṭapūra, and ghārtika are names for ghee-filled cakes or pastries.
Camasī is a roll of dough; baṭaka is avasekima, a preparation to be sprinkled or soaked.

children.text: bhṛṣṭā yavāḥ punardhānā dhānācūrṇaṃ tu saktavaḥ
children.translated_text: Roasted barley grains are punardhāna; flour made from grain is saktu.
Pṛthuka and cipuṭa are equivalent terms for flattened grain; lājā are parched grains, and akṣata are unbroken grains.
Wheat flour is samitā; ground barley is cikkasa.

children.text: guḍa ikṣurasaḥ kvāthaḥ śarkarā tu sitopalā ||
children.translated_text: Guḍa is a boiled preparation of sugarcane juice; śarkarā is sitopalā, crystalline sugar.
Sitā is sugar; madhudhūli is khaṇḍa, and khaṇḍa is another derivative of it.

children.text: matsyaṇḍī phāṇitaṃ cāpi rasālāyāṃ tu mārjitā ||
children.translated_text: Matsyaṇḍī and phāṇita are also sugarcane preparations; in rasālā the term mārjitā is used.

children.text: śikhariṇyatha yūryūṣo raso dugdhaṃ tu somajam
children.translated_text: Śikhariṇī is another name for rasālā; yūṣa is broth or juice, and dugdha, milk, is somaja.
Gorasa, kṣīra, ūdhasya, stanya, puṃsavana, and payas are names for milk.
Payasya denotes milk-products such as ghee and curds; peyūṣa is fresh milk.

children.text: ubhe kṣīrasya vikṛtī kilāṭī kūrcikāpi ca ||
children.translated_text: Kilāṭa and kūrcikā are both preparations or transformations of milk.
Pāyasa and paramānna are milk-rice; kṣīreyī and kṣīraja are names for curds made from milk.
Gorasa is another term for the milk product; its thickened form is also called drapsa and pattrala.
Ghṛta, haviṣya, ājya, havis, āghāra, and sarpis are names for ghee.
Ghee produced from yesterday's cow-milking is haiyaṃgavīna, while that produced in autumn is śaraja.
Dadhisāra, takrasāra, navanīta, and navoddhṛta denote fresh butter, the essence of curd or buttermilk.
For a milk product beaten with a churning-stick, kālaseya, ghola, and ariṣṭa are terms.
Rasāyana is one name; when mixed with half water, it is udaśvit, also called śveta and samodaka.
Takra is buttermilk with a quarter part water; mathita is churned buttermilk without water.
Prepared respectively with ghee and with curd, it is called sārpiṣka and dādhika.
When prepared with salt and with water, the terms are lāvaṇika and udaśvit respectively.
Audaśvita and audaśvitka are forms of udaśvit; when salt is present, it is called lāvaṇa.
Paiṭhara and ukhya denote what is cooked in a pot, and prayasta means well prepared.

children.text: pakve rāddhaṃ ca siddhaṃ ca bhṛṣṭaṃ pakvaṃ vināmbunā
children.translated_text: When cooked it is rāddha or siddha; bhṛṣṭa means cooked without water, that is, roasted or fried.
Roasted meat is called bhaṭitra; the same is also bhūti or bharūṭaka.

children.text: śūlyaṃ śūlākṛtaṃ māṃsaṃ niṣkvātho rasakaḥ samau
children.translated_text: Meat cooked on a spit is śūlya or śūlākṛta; niṣkvātha and rasaka are equivalent terms for broth.
Praṇīta and upasaṃpanna mean well prepared; masṛṇa and cikkaṇa mean smooth or unctuous.

children.text: picchilaṃ tu vijivilaṃ vijjalaṃ vijalaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: Picchila, vijivila, vijjala, and vijala all denote something slimy or sticky.
Bhāvita means vāsita, perfumed or steeped; saṃmṛṣṭa and śodhita are equivalent terms for cleaned or purified.
Kāñcika, kāñjika, dhānyāmla, āranāla, and tuṣodaka denote sour grain-water or fermented sour gruel.
Kulmāṣa, abhiṣuta, avantisoma, śukta, and kuñjala are names for such sour ferment.
Cukra, dhātughna, unnāha, rakṣoghna, and kuṇḍagolaka are further names for sour ferment or vinegar.
Mahārasa, suvīrāmla, sauvīra, and mrakṣaṇa are additional names for it.
Taila, sneha, and abhyañjana denote oil; veṣavāra and upaskara denote seasoning or condiment.
For amlavetasa, the sour tree product, the terms are tintiḍīka, cukra, and vṛkṣāmla.
Haridrā, kāñcanī, pītā, niśā, and varavarṇinī are names for turmeric.
Kṣava and kṣutābhijanana denote what causes sneezing; rājikā and rājasarṣapa denote mustard.

children.text: āsurī kṛṣṇikā cāsau kustumburu tu dhānyakam
children.translated_text: Āsurī and kṛṣṇikā also denote that mustard; kustumburu is dhānyaka, coriander.
Dhanyā, dhanyāka, and dhānyāka are names for coriander; marīca is black pepper, here called kṛṣṇamūṣaṇa.
Kolaka, vellaja, dhārmapattana, and yavanapriya are further names for black pepper.
Śuṇṭhī, mahauṣadhī, viśvā, nāgara, and viśvabheṣaja are names for dry ginger.
Vaidehī, pippalī, kṛṣṇā, upakulyā, māgadhī, and kaṇā denote long pepper.
The root of that long pepper is called granthika, sarvagranthika, and caṭakāśiras.
Trikaṭu, tryūṣaṇa, and vyoṣa denote the three pungent spices; ajājī, jīraka, and kaṇā denote cumin.
Sahasravedhi, vāhlīka, jatuka, hiṅgu, and rāmaṭha are names for asafoetida.
Nyāda, svadana, khādana, aśana, nighasa, valbhana, and abhyavahāra denote eating.
Jagdhi, jakṣaṇa, bhakṣaṇa, leha, pratyavasāna, ghasi, and āhāra are also terms for eating or taking food.
The damaged readings psāna, avaṣvāṇa, and viṣvāṇa, together with bhojana and jemana, are given as terms for eating or consumption.
Carvaṇa and cūrṇana mean chewing, the crushing done with the teeth; tasting with the tongue is lehana, licking.
Kalpavarta and prātarāśa mean breakfast; sagdhi means eating together.

children.text: grāso guḍerakaḥ piṇḍo gaḍolaḥ kavako guḍaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A mouthful is called grāsa, guḍeraka, piṇḍa, gaḍola, kavaka, or guḍa.
Gaṇḍola and kavala are also terms for a mouthful; for one satisfied, the terms are āghrāta, suhita, and āśita.
Tṛpti, sauhitya, and āghrāṇa denote satiety; next come terms for what is left after eating.
Phelā, piṇḍolī, and phelī denote food left after eating; then come terms for one who fills his own belly.
Kukṣiṃbhari, ātmaṃbhari, and udaraṃbhari denote one who fills his own belly.
Ādyūna and audarika denote a belly-centered person, one without higher ambition.
Udarapiśāca, sarvānnīna, and sarvānnabhakṣaka mean one who eats every kind of food.
Śāṣkula denotes a meat-eater; unmadiṣṇu means one afflicted with madness.
Gṛdhnu and gardhana mean greedy; tṛṣṇālu, glipsu, lubdha, and abhilāṣuka mean desirous or covetous.

children.text: lolupo lolubho lobhastṛṣṇā lipsā vaśaḥ spṛhā
children.translated_text: Lolupa and lolubha mean greedy; lobha, tṛṣṇā, lipsā, vaśa, and spṛhā denote greed or longing.
Kāṅkṣā, āśaṃsā, gardha, vāñchā, icchā, īhā, tṛṣṇā, and manoratha are further terms for desire.
Kāma and abhilāṣa also mean desire; abhidhyā is coveting another's property, and uddhata means insolent.
Avinīta means undisciplined; vinīta, nibhṛta, and praśrita mean disciplined, restrained, or humble.
For one obedient, the term is vinayastha; āśrava means one who stands by another's word.
Vaśya and praṇeya mean tractable or governable; dhṛṣṭa, viyāta, dhṛṣṇu, and dhṛṣṇaja mean bold or impudent.
Vīkṣāpanna and vilakṣa mean abashed; for one lacking boldness, the terms are śālīna and śārada.
Śubhaṃyu means endowed with auspiciousness; ahaṃyu means self-important or arrogant.
Kāmuka, kamitā, kamra, anuka, kāmayitā, and abhika mean amorous or desirous.
Kāmana, kamara, and abhīka are further terms for an amorous person; pañcabhadra means vipluta, disordered or overwhelmed.
Vyasanin denotes one beset by vice or misfortune; harṣamāṇa, pramanas, and hṛṣṭamānasa mean joyful in mind.
Vikurvāṇa and vicetas mean mentally altered; duranta and viparomanas mean perverse-minded.
For an intoxicated person the terms are śauṇḍa, utkaṭa, and kṣība; utka, utsuka, and unmanas mean eager or unsettled.
Utkaṇṭhita means longing; for one accused or censured, the terms are vācya, kṣārita, and dūṣita.
One known by his qualities is called āhatalakṣaṇa or kṛtalakṣaṇa.
Nirlakṣaṇa means without distinguishing marks; pāṇḍurapṛṣṭha and saṃkasuka mean unstable.
Tūṣṇīka means habitually silent; vivaśa means powerless, with impaired or ill-directed judgment.

children.text: baddho nigaḍito naddhaḥ kīlito yantritaḥ sitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Baddha, nigaḍita, naddha, kīlita, yantrita, and sita all mean bound or fettered.
Saṃdānita and saṃyata also mean bound; uddāna denotes a bond or fetter.
Manohata, pratihata, pratibaddha, and hata mean checked, obstructed, or thwarted.
Pratikṣipta and adhikṣipta mean rejected or censured; avakuṣṭa and niṣkāsita are equivalent terms for expelled.
Abhibhūta and apadhvasta mean overpowered or ruined; nyakkṛta and dhikkṛta mean humiliated or despised.
Nikṛta and viprakṛta mean injured or badly treated; nyakkāra and tiraskriyā denote contempt or rejection.
Paribhāva and viprakāra denote insult or ill-treatment; parāparya and abhitobhava are further terms for such humiliation.
Atyākāra and nikāra also mean insult; vipralabdha means deceived.
The damaged form svapnakśayālu and nidrālu mean sleepy; ghūrṇita and pracalāyita mean reeling or nodding with drowsiness.
Nidrāṇa, śayita, and supta mean asleep; jāgarūka and jāgarin mean awake or watchful.
Jāgaryā, jāgaraṇa, jāgarā, and jāgara denote wakefulness.
Viṣvagañcati and viṣvadryañc mean going or turned in all directions; devadryañc and devamañcati mean going or turned toward the gods.
<s>Sadhryaṅ</s> is something that goes together; <s>tiryaṅ</s> is something that goes across or obliquely.
<s>Saṃśayālu</s> and <s>saṃśayitā</s> mean a doubter; <s>gṛhayālu</s> denotes one who grasps.
<s>Patayālu</s> and <s>pātuka</s> mean prone to falling; <s>rociṣṇu</s> and <s>rocana</s> are equivalent, meaning shining or pleasing.
<s>Dakṣiṇya</s> and <s>dakṣiṇīya</s> denote one deserving a <s>dakṣiṇā</s> (honorarium); then <s>daṇḍita</s> means punished or fined.
<s>Dāpita</s> and <s>sādhita</s> also denote one who has been made to pay or subdued; <s>arcya</s>, <s>pratīkṣya</s>, <s>pūjita</s>, and <s>arhita</s> denote one fit to be honored.
<s>Namasyita</s>, <s>namasita</s>, <s>apacita</s>, <s>avañcita</s>, and <s>arcita</s> mean worshipped or honored.
<s>Pūjā</s>, <s>arhaṇā</s>, <s>saparyā</s>, and <s>arcā</s> denote worship; <s>upahāra</s> and <s>bali</s> both mean an offering.

children.text: viklavo vihvalaḥ sthūlaḥ pīvā pīnaśca pīvaraḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Viklava</s> and <s>vihvala</s> mean distraught or bewildered; <s>sthūla</s>, <s>pīvā</s>, <s>pīna</s>, and <s>pīvara</s> mean stout or well-nourished.
<s>Cakṣuṣya</s> and <s>subhaga</s> mean pleasing to the eye or beautiful; <s>dveṣya</s> means hateful, <s>akṣigata</s> means visible or before the eyes, and <s>aṃsala</s> means strong.
<s>Nirdagdha</s> means completely burnt; <s>māṃsala</s> and <s>upacita</s> mean fleshy or filled out; <s>durbala</s> and <s>kṛśa</s> mean weak or thin.
<s>Kṣāma</s>, <s>kṣīṇa</s>, <s>tanu</s>, <s>chāta</s>, <s>stalina</s>, <s>amāṃsa</s>, and <s>pelava</s> are terms for the emaciated or thin.
<s>Picaṇḍila</s> means large-bellied; <s>tundi</s>, <s>tundika</s>, and <s>tundila</s> also denote a pot-bellied person.
<s>Udarin</s> and <s>udarila</s> are belly-related terms; <s>vikha</s>, <s>vikhu</s>, and <s>vigra</s> denote one without a nose.
<s>Avanāṭa</s>, <s>avaṭīṭa</s>, and <s>ababhraṭa</s> denote a person with a bent or depressed nose.
<s>Kharaṇa</s> and <s>kharaṇasa</s> denote one with a rough or harsh nose; <s>naḥkṣudra</s> denotes one with a small nose.
<s>Khuraṇa</s> is <s>suraṇasa</s>, while <s>unnasa</s> means one with a high or prominent nose.
<s>Paṅgu</s> and <s>śroṇa</s> mean lame or crippled; <s>khalati</s>, <s>khalvāṭa</s>, and <s>aindraluptika</s> mean bald.
<s>Śipiviṣṭa</s> and <s>babhru</s> mean tawny or brown; <s>kāṇa</s>, <s>kanana</s>, and <s>ekadṛk</s> denote one-eyed.
<s>Pṛśri</s> denotes one with a small body; <s>gaḍula</s> denotes a hunchback; <s>kuṇi</s> denotes one with a deformed hand.
<s>Nikharva</s>, <s>khaṭṭana</s>, <s>kharva</s>, <s>kharvaśākha</s>, and <s>vāmana</s> mean dwarf or short-limbed.

children.text: akarṇa eḍo badhiro duścarmā tu dvinagnakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Akarṇa</s> and <s>eḍa</s> denote one without ears; <s>badhira</s> means deaf, and <s>duścarman</s> or <s>dvinagnaka</s> one with diseased skin.
<s>Vaṇḍa</s> means a castrate or eunuch, and <s>śipiviṣṭa</s> another marked bodily condition; <s>khoḍa</s> and <s>khora</s> denote a lame person.
<s>Vikalāṅga</s> means maimed; <s>pogaṇḍa</s>, <s>ūrdhvajñu</s>, and <s>ūrdhvajānuka</s> denote one whose knees are drawn upward.
<s>Ūrdhvajña</s> is another such term; <s>prajñu</s> and <s>prajña</s> denote one with widely separated knees.
<s>Saṃjñu</s> and <s>saṃjña</s> denote one whose knees touch; <s>balina</s> and <s>balibha</s> are equivalent, meaning strong.
<s>Udagradanta</s> or <s>dantura</s> means protruding-toothed; <s>muṣkara</s> denotes one with hanging testicles.
<s>Andha</s> and <s>gatākṣa</s> mean blind; <s>utpaśya</s> or <s>unmukha</s> means looking upward, while <s>avāṅ</s> means face downward.

children.text: muṇḍastu muṇḍitaḥ keśī keśavaḥ keśiko 'pi ca
children.translated_text: <s>Muṇḍa</s> and <s>muṇḍita</s> mean shaven-headed; <s>keśī</s>, <s>keśava</s>, and <s>keśika</s> mean haired or long-haired.
<s>Valira</s> and <s>kekara</s> denote squint-eyed; <s>tuṇḍila</s> and <s>tuṇḍibha</s> denote one with a large navel or belly.
<s>Āmayāvin</s>, <s>apaṭu</s>, <s>glāna</s>, <s>glāsura</s>, <s>vikṛta</s>, and <s>ātura</s> mean sick, feeble, or distressed.
<s>Vyādhita</s>, <s>abhyamita</s>, and <s>abhyānta</s> mean afflicted by disease; <s>dadruṇa</s> denotes one suffering from <s>dadru</s> (ringworm or eczema).
<s>Pāmana</s> and <s>kacchura</s> are equivalent terms for one affected by itch or scabies; <s>sātisāra</s> and <s>atisārakī</s> denote one with diarrhea.
<s>Vātakī</s> or <s>vātarogī</s> denotes one afflicted by a wind-disorder; <s>śleṣmata</s>, <s>śleṣmaṇa</s>, and <s>kaphī</s> denote one with phlegm.
<s>Cilla</s> and <s>culla</s> mean one with moist or weeping eyes; <s>pilla</s> denotes one affected in the eyes, and <s>arśoyuj</s> or <s>arśasa</s> one with piles.
<s>Mūrta</s> and <s>mūrchāla</s> denote one fainted or unconscious; <s>sidhmala</s> denotes one affected by <s>sidhma</s>, as <s>kilāsin</s> does.

children.text: pittaṃ māyuḥ kaphaḥ śleṣmā balāśaḥ snehabhūḥ khaṭa:
children.translated_text: <s>Pitta</s> is also <s>māyu</s>; <s>kapha</s> is <s>śleṣman</s>, <s>balāśa</s>, <s>snehabhū</s>, and <s>khaṭa</s>.
<s>Roga</s>, <s>rujā</s>, <s>rug</s>, <s>ātaṅka</s>, <s>māndya</s>, <s>vyādhi</s>, and <s>apāṭava</s> denote disease or infirmity.
<s>Āma</s>, <s>āmaya</s>, <s>ākalya</s>, <s>upatāpa</s>, and <s>gada</s> are likewise terms for illness.

children.text: kṣayaḥ śoṣo rājayakṣmā yakṣmātha kṣutkṣutaṃ kṣavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kṣaya</s>, <s>śoṣa</s>, <s>rājayakṣmā</s>, and <s>yakṣmā</s> denote consumption; <s>kṣut</s>, <s>kṣuta</s>, and <s>kṣava</s> denote a sneeze.
<s>Kāsa</s> denotes cough and <s>kṣavathu</s> sneezing; <s>pāmā</s>, <s>khasa</s>, <s>kacchū</s>, and <s>vicarcikā</s> denote itch or scabies.

children.text: kaṇḍūḥ kaṇḍūyanaṃ kharjūḥ kaṇḍūyātha kṣataṃ vraṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kaṇḍū</s>, <s>kaṇḍūyana</s>, <s>kharjū</s>, and <s>kaṇḍūyā</s> mean itching; <s>kṣata</s> and <s>vraṇa</s> mean a wound.
<s>Arus</s>, <s>īrma</s>, and <s>kṣaṇatu</s> are wound terms; the mark of a healed wound is <s>kiṇa</s>.
<s>Ślīpada</s>, <s>pādavalmīka</s>, <s>pādasphoṭa</s>, and <s>vipādikā</s> denote diseases or eruptions of the foot.
<s>Sphoṭaka</s>, <s>piḍaka</s>, and <s>gaṇḍa</s> denote a boil, pustule, or swelling; <s>pṛṣṭagranthi</s> and <s>gaḍu</s> denote a knot or tumor on the back.
<s>Śvitra</s>, <s>pāṇḍura</s>, and <s>kuṣṭa</s> denote white skin disease or leprosy; <s>keśaghna</s> is <s>indraluptaka</s>, loss of hair.

children.text: sidhma kilāsaṃ tvakpuṣpaṃ sidhmaṃ koṭhastu maṇḍalam
children.translated_text: <s>Sidhma</s>, <s>kilāsa</s>, and <s>tvakpuṣpa</s> denote a blotchy skin disease; <s>koṭha</s> is <s>maṇḍala</s>, a circular eruption.
<s>Gaṇḍamālā</s> denotes <s>galagaṇḍa</s>, swelling of the neck; <s>rohiṇī</s> is <s>galāṅkura</s>, a growth or disease of the throat.

children.text: hikkā hekkā ca hṛllāsaḥ pratiśyāyastu pīnasaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Hikkā</s> and <s>hekkā</s> mean hiccup; <s>hṛllāsa</s> means nausea, and <s>pratiśyāya</s> is <s>pīnasa</s>, nasal catarrh.
<s>Śotha</s> and <s>śvayathu</s> mean swelling; <s>durnāman</s>, <s>arśas</s>, and <s>gudāṅkura</s> denote piles or hemorrhoids.
<s>Chardā</s>, <s>pracchardikā</s>, <s>chardi</s>, <s>vamathu</s>, <s>vamana</s>, and <s>vami</s> denote vomiting.
<s>Gulma</s> is an abdominal lump or tumor, <s>udaragranthi</s>; <s>udāvarta</s> is <s>gudagraha</s>, obstruction of the bowels.
<s>Gati</s> denotes a sinus wound, <s>nāḍīvraṇa</s>; <s>vṛddhi</s> and <s>kuruṇḍa</s> denote enlargement of the testicles.
<s>Aśmarī</s> denotes urinary stone and belongs among urinary difficulty; <s>prameha</s> means excessive urination.
<s>Anāha</s> is <s>nibandha</s>, constipation or obstruction; <s>grahaṇī</s> and <s>rukpravāhikā</s> denote painful intestinal disease or dysentery.
The varieties of disease include <s>vidradhi</s> (abscess), <s>bhagaṃdara</s> (fistula), <s>jvara</s> (fever), and the like.
<s>Doṣajña</s>, <s>bhiṣaj</s>, <s>vaidya</s>, <s>āyurvedī</s>, and <s>cikitsaka</s> denote a physician.
<s>Rogahārin</s> and <s>agadaṃkāra</s> mean remover of disease; <s>bheṣaja</s>, <s>tantra</s>, and <s>auṣadha</s> denote a remedy or medicine.
<s>Bhaiṣajya</s>, <s>agada</s>, and <s>jāyu</s> are medicines; <s>cikitsā</s> is counteraction of disease, treatment.
<s>Upacaryā</s> and <s>upacāra</s> mean medical care or treatment; <s>laṅghana</s> is <s>apatarpaṇa</s>, depletion or fasting therapy.
<s>Jāṅgulika</s> is a poison-healer, <s>viṣabhiṣaj</s>; <s>svāsthya</s>, <s>vārta</s>, and <s>anāmaya</s> denote health.
<s>Sahya</s> and <s>ārogya</s> mean wellness; <s>paṭu</s>, <s>ullāgha</s>, <s>vārta</s>, and <s>kalya</s> denote one free from disease.
<s>Kusṛtyā</s> denotes bad conduct; <s>pārśvaka</s> and <s>saṃdhijīvaka</s> denote one who seeks wealth through such expedients.

children.text: satkṛtyālaṃkṛtāṃ kanyāṃ yo dadāti sa kūkudaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A man who gives a girl in marriage after honoring and adorning her is called <s>kūkuda</s>.
<s>Capala</s> and <s>cikura</s> mean fickle; <s>nīlīrāga</s> denotes attachment like indigo dye, a steady affection.
<s>Haridrārāga</s> is another, less lasting kind of coloring or attachment; <s>medura</s> means dense and oily, or richly affectionate.
<s>Gehenardī</s>, <s>geheśūra</s>, <s>piṇḍīśūra</s>, and <s>astimāndhanī</s> are names for one whose courage is confined to the house or to food.
<s>Goṣṭhaśva</s> denotes one who, staying in his own place, shows hostility to others; next comes the sense 'standing in calamity.'
One in calamity is <s>āpanna</s>; <s>āpad</s>, <s>vipatti</s>, and <s>vipat</s> mean misfortune, while <s>snigdha</s> and <s>vatsala</s> mean affectionate.
<s>Upādhi</s> and <s>abhyāgārika</s> denote a man occupied with family or household affairs.
<s>Jaivātṛka</s> means long-lived; <s>śaṅkura</s> means causing fear.
<s>Abhipanna</s> means one seeking refuge; <s>kāraṇika</s> means an examiner or investigator.
<s>Samardhuka</s> means a boon-giver; <s>vrātin</s> denotes people who live in a band or community.
<s>Sabhya</s>, <s>sadasya</s>, <s>pārṣadya</s>, <s>sabhāstāra</s>, and <s>sabhāsad</s> denote members of an assembly.
<s>Sāmājika</s> is also an assembly-member; <s>sabhā</s>, <s>saṃsat</s>, <s>samāja</s>, <s>pariṣat</s>, and <s>sadas</s> denote an assembly.
<s>Parṣat</s>, <s>samajyā</s>, <s>goṣṭhī</s>, <s>āsthā</s>, <s>āsthāna</s>, <s>samiti</s>, and <s>ghaṭā</s> also denote an assembly or gathering.
<s>Sāṃvatsara</s>, <s>jyautiṣika</s>, <s>mauhūrtika</s>, and <s>nimittavit</s> denote an astrologer or knower of omens.
<s>Daivajña</s>, <s>gaṇaka</s>, <s>ādeśin</s>, <s>jñānin</s>, and <s>kārtāntika</s> too denote diviners or astrologers.
<s>Vipraśnika</s> and <s>īkṣaṇika</s> also do so; a <s>saiddhāntika</s> is a <s>tāntrika</s>, one versed in technical doctrine.
For a writer, terms beginning with <s>akṣara</s> are used, as well as <s>caṇa</s>, <s>jīvaka</s>, and <s>cañcu</s>.
A scribe is <s>vārṇika</s> and <s>lipikara</s>; the setting down of letters is <s>akṣaranyāsa</s>, <s>lipi</s>, or <s>livi</s>.
<s>Maṣidhāna</s> and <s>maṣikūpī</s> are ink-pots; <s>malināmbu</s> and <s>maṣī</s> denote ink.
A <s>kalika</s> is a <s>kulaśreṣṭhin</s>, a chief of a family or guild; a <s>sabhika</s> is an organizer of gambling.
In dice-play, <s>kitava</s>, <s>dyūtakṛt</s>, <s>dhūrta</s>, and <s>akṣadhūrta</s> denote a gambler or cheat.
<s>Durodara</s>, <s>kaitava</s>, <s>dyūta</s>, and <s>akṣavatī</s> mean gambling; <s>paṇa</s> is a stake.
The dice are <s>pāśaka</s>, <s>pāsaka</s>, and <s>akṣa</s>; the playing is <s>devana</s>, and its stake is <s>glaha</s>.
<s>Aṣṭāpada</s> is the gaming board; <s>śāriphala</s>, <s>śāra</s>, <s>śāri</s>, and <s>khelanī</s> denote game-pieces.
<s>Pariṇāya</s> is the moving of the pieces all around.
<s>Samāhvaya</s> is gambling with living beings; a snake-catcher is <s>vyālagrāhin</s> or <s>ahituṇḍika</s>.
One swift as thought is <s>manojavas</s>; one like a father is <s>tātatulya</s>; an instructor is <s>śāstā</s> or <s>deśaka</s>.
<s>Sukṛtin</s>, <s>puṇyavat</s>, and <s>dhanya</s> mean meritorious or fortunate; <s>mitrayu</s> is <s>mitravatsala</s>, fond of friends.
<s>Kṣemaṃkara</s>, <s>ariṣṭatāti</s>, <s>śivatāti</s>, and <s>śivaṃkara</s> mean one who brings welfare.
<s>Śraddhālu</s>, <s>āstika</s>, and <s>śrāddha</s> mean believing or faithful; <s>nāstika</s> is the opposite.
<s>Vairaṅgika</s> is fit for dispassion; one free from deceit is <s>vītadambha</s> or <s>akalkana</s>.
<s>Praṇāyya</s> denotes one to be trusted; <s>asaṃmata</s> one not approved; <s>anveṣṭṛ</s> a seeker; <s>anupadī</s> a follower; <s>saha</s> is <s>kṣama</s>, enduring.
<s>Śakta</s> and <s>prabhūṣṇu</s> mean capable; one possessed by spirits is <s>bhūtātta</s> or <s>āviṣṭa</s>; loose is <s>śithila</s> or <s>ślatha</s>.
<s>Saṃvāhaka</s> is <s>aṅgamarda</s>, a body-massager; one whose seed is lost is <s>naṣṭabīja</s> or <s>niṣkala</s>.
<s>Āsīna</s> means seated, <s>upaviṣṭa</s>; <s>ūrdhva</s>, <s>ūrdhvaṃdama</s>, and <s>sthita</s> mean standing.
<s>Adhvanīna</s>, <s>adhvaga</s>, <s>adhvanya</s>, <s>pāntha</s>, <s>pathika</s>, and <s>deśika</s> denote a traveler.

children.text: pravāsī tadguṇo hāriḥ pātheyaṃ śambalaṃ same ||
children.translated_text: <s>Pravāsin</s> is one who is abroad; <s>hārin</s> has that quality; <s>pātheya</s> and <s>śambala</s> are provisions for a journey.
<s>Jaṅghāla</s>, <s>atijava</s>, <s>jaṅghākarika</s>, <s>jāṅghika</s>, and <s>javin</s> mean very swift.
<s>Javana</s> means swift; <s>vega</s>, <s>raya</s>, <s>raṃhas</s>, <s>tara</s>, and <s>syada</s> denote speed.

children.text: javo vāja: prasaraśca mandagāmī tu mantharaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Java</s>, <s>vāja</s>, and <s>prasara</s> also denote speed; a slow-going one is <s>mandagāmin</s> or <s>manthara</s>.
<s>Kāmaṃgāmin</s>, <s>anugāmin</s>, <s>atyantin</s>, and <s>atyantagāmin</s> denote one who goes at will, follows, or goes to the very end.
<s>Sahāya</s> and <s>abhicara</s> mean companion; related travelling or conveyance terms include <s>jīvin</s>, <s>gāmin</s>, <s>cara</s>, and <s>plava</s>.
<s>Sevaka</s> is a servant; service is <s>sevā</s>, <s>bhakti</s>, <s>paricaryā</s>, and <s>prasādanā</s>.
<s>Śuśrūṣā</s>, <s>ārādhana</s>, <s>upāsti</s>, <s>varivasyā</s>, and <s>parīṣṭi</s> also denote service or attendance.
<s>Upacāra</s> is attendance; a foot-soldier is <s>padāti</s>, <s>patti</s>, <s>padga</s>, or <s>padātika</s>.
<s>Pādātika</s>, <s>pādacārin</s>, <s>padājin</s>, and <s>padika</s> also denote a pedestrian or foot-soldier.
<s>Puras</s>, <s>agratas</s>, <s>agre</s>, and <s>purastāt</s> mean 'in front'; one going before is <s>purastogama</s>, <s>gāmin</s>, or <s>gā</s>.
<s>Praṣṭha</s> denotes the rear; then <s>āveśika</s>, <s>āgantu</s>, <s>praghuṇa</s>, <s>abhyāgata</s>, and <s>atithi</s> denote a guest or arrival.
<s>Prāghūrṇika</s> too denotes a guest; <s>āveśika</s>, <s>ātithya</s>, and <s>ātitheya</s> denote hospitality.

children.text: sūryoḍhastu sa saṃprāpto yaḥ sūrye 'staṃ gate tithiḥ
children.translated_text: A <s>sūryoḍha</s> guest is one who has arrived after the sun has set.
<s>Pādya</s> is water for the feet; <s>arghya</s> is water for an offering; <s>gaurava</s> is respectful honor.
<s>Abhyutthāna</s> is rising up; one who causes pain is <s>vyathaka</s>, and one who touches a vulnerable spot is <s>marmaspṛś</s> or <s>aruṃtuda</s>.

children.text: grāmeyake tu grāmīṇagrāmyau loko janaḥ prajāḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Grāmīṇa</s> and <s>grāmya</s> mean rustic or belonging to a village; <s>loka</s>, <s>jana</s>, and <s>prajā</s> denote people.
<s>Āmuṣyāyaṇa</s> means 'son of such-and-such a man'; one with a famous father is <s>prakhyātavaptṛka</s>.
<s>Kulya</s>, <s>kulīna</s>, <s>abhijāta</s>, <s>kauleyaka</s>, and <s>mahākula</s> mean well-born.
<s>Jātya</s> means noble by birth; lineage is <s>gotra</s>, <s>saṃtāna</s>, <s>anvavāya</s>, <s>abhijana</s>, and <s>kula</s>.

children.text: anvayo jananaṃ vaṃśaḥ strī nārī vanitā vadhūḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Anvaya</s>, <s>janana</s>, and <s>vaṃśa</s> also mean lineage; a woman is <s>strī</s>, <s>nārī</s>, <s>vanitā</s>, or <s>vadhū</s>.
<s>Vaśā</s>, <s>sīmantinī</s>, <s>vāmā</s>, <s>varṇinī</s>, <s>mahilā</s>, and <s>abalā</s> also denote a woman.
<s>Yoṣā</s> and <s>yoṣit</s> likewise mean woman; particular kinds of women are <s>kāntā</s>, <s>bhīru</s>, and <s>nitambinī</s>.
<s>Pramadā</s>, <s>sundarī</s>, <s>rāmā</s>, <s>ramaṇī</s>, <s>lalanā</s>, and <s>aṅganā</s> are further terms for a woman, especially a lovely woman.
A woman may be specified by her own quality, by comparison, or by words such as <s>manojñā</s>.
A woman may be qualified by the action or quality of a limb, as in <s>taralalocanā</s>, 'one with darting eyes'.
So too <s>alasekṣaṇā</s>, 'languid-eyed', <s>mṛgākṣī</s>, 'doe-eyed', and <s>mattebhagamanā</s>, 'moving like a rutting elephant'.
<s>Vāmākṣī</s>, 'lovely-eyed', and <s>susmitāsyā</s>, 'with a beautifully smiling face', are such; <s>māna</s>, <s>līlā</s>, <s>smara</s>, and the like are their own traits.
<s>Līlā</s>, <s>vilāsa</s>, <s>vicchitti</s>, <s>vivvoka</s>, and <s>kilakiñcita</s>,
as well as <s>moṭṭāyita</s>, <s>kuṭṭamita</s>, <s>lalita</s>, and <s>vihṛta</s>,
and <s>vibhrama</s>: these are the ten natural ornaments of women.
<s>Prāgalbhya</s>, <s>audārya</s>, <s>mādhurya</s>, <s>śobhā</s>, <s>dhīratva</s>, and <s>kānti</s>,
together with <s>dīpti</s>, are spontaneous qualities; <s>bhāva</s>, <s>hāva</s>, and <s>helā</s> are the three arising from the body.

children.text: sā kopanā bhāminī syācchekā mattā ca vāṇinī
children.translated_text: An angry woman is <s>kopanā</s> or <s>bhāminī</s>; a clever or eloquent woman is <s>chekā</s>, <s>mattā</s>, or <s>vāṇinī</s>.

children.text: kanyā kanī kumārī ca gaurī tu nagnikārajāḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kanyā</s>, <s>kanī</s>, and <s>kumārī</s> mean maiden; <s>gaurī</s>, <s>nagnikā</s>, and <s>arajā</s> denote a girl before menstruation.
<s>Madhyamā</s> is one who has seen menstruation; <s>taruṇī</s>, <s>yuvatī</s>, and <s>carī</s> denote a young woman.
<s>Taluṇī</s>, <s>dikkarī</s>, <s>varyā</s>, <s>patiṃvarā</s>, and <s>svayaṃvarā</s> denote a marriageable woman or one choosing a husband.
<s>Suvāsinī</s> and <s>vadhūṭī</s> mean a married woman; <s>ciriṇṭī</s> likewise; then <s>sadharmiṇī</s>,
<s>patnī</s>, <s>sahacarī</s>, <s>pāṇigṛhītī</s>, <s>gṛhiṇī</s>, and <s>guhā</s> mean wife.

children.text: dārāḥ kṣetraṃ vadhūrbhāryā janī jāyā parigrahaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Dārāḥ</s>, <s>kṣetra</s>, <s>vadhū</s>, <s>bhāryā</s>, <s>janī</s>, <s>jāyā</s>, and <s>parigraha</s> also mean wife.

children.text: dvitīyoḍhā kalatraṃ ca puraṃdhrī tu kuṭumbinī ||
children.translated_text: <s>Dvitīyoḍhā</s> and <s>kalatra</s> too mean wife; <s>puraṃdhrī</s> is <s>kuṭumbinī</s>, a housewife.

children.text: prajāvatī bhrāturjāyā sūnoḥ snuṣā janī vabhūḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Prajāvatī</s> is a wife with children; a brother's wife is <s>bhrātṛjāyā</s>; a son's wife is <s>snuṣā</s>, <s>janī</s>, or <s>vabhū</s>.
The wives of a group of brothers are mutually called <s>yātaras</s>, co-sisters.
<s>Vīrapatnī</s> and <s>vīrabhāryā</s> mean the wife of a hero; <s>kulastrī</s> and <s>kulabālikā</s> mean a woman of good family.

children.text: preyasī dayitā kāntā prāṇeśā vallabhā priyā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Preyasī</s>, <s>dayitā</s>, <s>kāntā</s>, <s>prāṇeśā</s>, <s>vallabhā</s>, and <s>priyā</s> denote a beloved woman.

children.text: hṛdayeśā prāṇasamā śreṣṭhā praṇayaṇī ca sā
children.translated_text: She is also <s>hṛdayeśā</s>, <s>prāṇasamā</s>, <s>śreṣṭhā</s>, and <s>praṇayaṇī</s>.

children.text: preyasyādyāḥ puṃsi patyau bhartā sektā patirvaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: The terms beginning with <s>preyasī</s>, when masculine, denote a husband; <s>bhartṛ</s>, <s>sektṛ</s>, <s>pati</s>, and <s>vara</s> also mean husband.

children.text: vivoḍhā ramaṇo bhoktā rucyo varayitā dhavaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Vivoḍhṛ</s>, <s>ramaṇa</s>, <s>bhoktṛ</s>, <s>rucya</s>, <s>varayitṛ</s>, and <s>dhava</s> likewise denote a husband or lover.
<s>Janya</s> denotes his friends or marriage-party; marriage is <s>vivāha</s> and <s>pāṇipīḍana</s>.
<s>Pāṇigrahaṇa</s>, <s>udvāha</s>, <s>upayāma</s>, and <s>ayamā</s> also mean marriage.
<s>Dārakarman</s> and <s>pariṇaya</s> also denote marriage; a daughter's husband is <s>jāmātṛ</s>.
<s>Upapati</s>, <s>jāra</s>, and <s>bhujaṅga</s> mean a paramour; <s>gaṇikāpati</s> is the keeper or lover of a courtesan.
<s>Jampatī</s>, <s>dampatī</s>, <s>bhāryāpatī</s>, and <s>jāyāpatī</s> equally denote a married couple.

children.text: yautakaṃ yutayordeyaṃ sudāyo haraṇaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: <s>Yautaka</s> is what is to be given to the joined pair; that gift is also <s>sudāya</s> and <s>haraṇa</s>.
A consecrated queen is <s>mahiṣī</s>; the other women of a king are <s>bhoginī</s>s.
<s>Sairandhrī</s> is a woman living in another's house, independent, and making a living by a craft.
Asiknī, antaḥpura-preṣyā, dūtī, and saṃcārikā are equivalent terms for a female messenger or attendant of the inner quarters.

children.text: prājñī prajñā prajānantyāṃ prājñā tu prajñayānvitā
children.translated_text: Prājñī and prajñā denote a woman who understands; prājñā, however, is one endowed with wisdom.
Ābhīrī and mahāśūdrī are used alike, whether by birth-caste or by connection with a man of that group.
In relation to a male, ācāryānī is the wife of an ācārya; mātulānī and mātulī denote the maternal uncle's wife.
Upādhyāyānī and upādhyāyī denote a preceptor's wife; similarly there are the forms kṣatriyī, āryī, and śūdrī.
By her own status the forms are ācāryā, śūdrā, and kṣatriyā, and also akṣatriyāṇī.
Upādhyāyī and upādhyāyā may denote a female teacher; āryā and āryāṇī are again equivalent forms.
A didhiṣū is a punarbhū, a woman married again, also called dvirūḍhā; her husband is called didhiṣu.
That twice-born man is called agredidhiṣu when just such a woman is his wife.
When the elder brother is unmarried, the younger brother who takes a wife is called parivettṛ.
His elder brother is parivitti, and the wife is called parivedinī.
A woman eager for sexual union is vṛṣasyantī or kāmukī; one possessed by desire is kāmukā.
A woman for whom a co-wife has been made is kṛtasāpatnikā and adhivinnā; next come terms for a devoted wife.
Ekapatnī, sucaritrā, sādhvī, satī, and satītvarī denote a faithful and well-conducted wife.
Puṃścalī, carṣaṇī, bandhaky, avinītā, and pāṃśulā denote an unchaste or wanton woman.

children.text: svairiṇī kulaṭā yāti yā priyaṃ sābhisārikā
children.translated_text: Svairiṇī and kulaṭā are such a woman; one who goes to her lover is an abhisārikā.

children.text: vayasyāliḥ sakhī sadhrīcyaśiśvī tu śiśuṃ vinā ||
children.translated_text: Vayasyā, āli, sakhī, and sadhrīcī denote a female friend; aśiśvī is a woman without a child.
Pativatnī means one whose husband is living; viśvastā and vidhavā are equivalent terms for a widow.
Nirvīrā is a woman without husband or son; jīvattokā and jīvasū denote one whose child is living.
Naśyatprasūtikā and nandu denote a woman whose offspring is lost; saśmaśru means bearded, and varamālinī means garlanded for the bridegroom.
Kātyāyinī denotes a half-aged woman; kāṣāyavasanā and adhavā denote a woman in ochre or without a husband.

children.text: śravaṇā bhikṣukī muṇḍā poṭā tu strīnṛlakṣaṇā
children.translated_text: Śravaṇā, bhikṣukī, and muṇḍā denote a shaven female mendicant; poṭā is one marked by both female and male characteristics.
Sādhāraṇastrī, gaṇikā, veśyā, paṇyā, and paṇāṅganā denote a common woman or prostitute.
Bhujiṣyā, lañjikā, rūpājīvā, and vāravadhū are further terms for a courtesan.

children.text: sā vāramukhyātha cundī kuṭṭanī śaṃbhalī samāḥ ||
children.translated_text: She is also vāramukhyā; cundī, kuṭṭanī, and śaṃbhalī are equivalent terms for a procuress.

children.text: poṭā voṭā ca ceṭī ca dāsī ca kuṭahārikā
children.translated_text: Poṭā, voṭā, ceṭī, dāsī, and kuṭahārikā denote a maidservant or female slave.

children.text: nagnā tu koṭavī vṛddhā paliknyatha rajasvalā ||
children.translated_text: A naked woman is koṭavī, and an old woman is paliknī; next come terms for a menstruating woman.
Puṣpavatī, adhirātreyī, strīdharmiṇī, and malinyavī denote a menstruating woman.

children.text: udakyā ṛtumatī ca puṣpahīnā tu niṣkalā ||
children.translated_text: Udakyā and ṛtumatī are also such terms; puṣpahīnā and niṣkalā denote a woman without menstrual flow.

children.text: rākā tu sarajāḥ kanyā strīdharmaḥ puṣpamārtavam
children.translated_text: Rākā is a maiden with menstrual blood; strīdharma, puṣpa, and ārtava denote menstruation.
Rajas is menstrual blood, and its proper time is ṛtu; surata, mohana, and rata denote sexual enjoyment.
Saṃveśana, saṃprayoga, saṃbhoga, and raho-rati are terms for sexual union.
Grāmyadharma, nidhuvana, kāmakeli, and paśukriyā are further terms for intercourse.

children.text: vyavāyo maithunaṃ strīpuṃsordvadvaṃ mithunaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: Vyavāya and maithuna denote the pairing or union of woman and man, also called dvandva and mithuna.
Antarvatnī, gurviṇī, garbhavatī, and udariṇī denote a pregnant woman.
Āpannasattvā and gurvī are also such terms; śraddhālu means one affected by pregnancy craving, endowed with dohada.

children.text: vijātā ca prajātā ca jātāpatyā prasūtikā ||
children.translated_text: Vijātā, prajātā, jātāpatyā, and prasūtikā denote a woman who has given birth.

children.text: garbhastu garabho bhrūṇo dohadalakṣaṇaṃ ca saḥ
children.translated_text: Garbha, garabha, and bhrūṇa denote the embryo or fetus, and it is characterized by dohada.
Garbhāśaya denotes the womb; jarāyu and ulva, and again kalala and ulva, are paired equivalent terms.
Dohada, daurhṛta, śraddhā, and lālasā denote pregnancy craving; sūti denotes childbirth.
Vaijanana, vijanana, prasava, and nandana are further terms for birth or delivery.
Aṅgātmaja, sūnu, tanaya, dāraka, and suta denote a son or child, along with udvaha.
For a son, and in the feminine for a daughter, toka, apatya, and prasūti are used as terms for offspring.
Toka and prajā apply to both sexes; bhrātrīya and bhrātṛvya denote a brother's son.
Svasrīya, bhāgineya, jāmeya, and kutapa denote a sister's son.

children.text: naptā pautraḥ putraputro dauhitro duhituḥ sutaḥ
children.translated_text: Naptṛ, pautra, and putraputra denote a son's son; dauhitra is a daughter's son.
Pratinaptṛ and prapautra denote a great-grandson; his son is called parampara.
Paitṛṣvaseya and paitṛṣvasrīya denote a child connected with the father's sister.
Mātṛṣvasrīya, like mātṛṣvaseya, denotes a child connected with the mother's sister.
Vimātṛja, vaimātreya, dvaimātura, and dvimātṛja denote one born from another mother or a stepmother.
For the son of a co-wife or stepmother, the terms sāṃmātura and avāṅmātura are given.
Saubhāgineya and kānīna are respectively the sons of a subhagā woman and of an unmarried maiden.
Paunarbhava and pārastraiṇeya are respectively the sons of a remarried woman and of another man's wife.
Dāsera and dāseya denote the son of a female slave; nāṭera is the son of an actress.
Bandhula and bāndhakineya denote the son of a kept woman, while kaulaṭera is the son of an unchaste woman.
Kaulaṭineya is likewise the term for one who is the son of a mendicant woman or an unchaste woman.
Both of these are called kaulaṭeya; kṣetraja is a son begotten by a brother-in-law or similar appointed man.
A son born from one's own wife is aurasa or orasya; a son of adultery after the husband's death is jāraja.
Such a child is golaka when the husband is dead, and kuṇḍa when he is alive; a brother is sahodara.
Samānodarya, sodarya, sagarbha, and sahaja also denote a brother born from the same womb.

children.text: sodaraśca sa tu jyeṣṭhaḥ syātpitryaḥ pūrvajo 'grajaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sodara is another term; when he is elder, he is jyeṣṭha, pitrya, pūrvaja, or agraja.
For one born later, the terms are yaviṣṭha, kaniṣṭha, avaraja, and anuja.
He is also yavīyān and kanīyān; pitṛvya, śyāla, and mātula are the respective uncles or in-law terms that follow.
They denote the brothers of one's father, wife, and mother respectively; devṛ and devara are terms for the husband's brother.
Devā too denotes the husband's younger brother; jāmi, bhaginī, and svasā denote a sister.
Nanāndā, nanandā, and nandinī denote the husband's sister.
The elder sister of one's wife is jyeṣṭhaśvaśrū or kulīcasā.
Her younger sister is śyālikā, hālī, yantraṇī, or kelikuñcikā.

children.text: kelirdravaḥ parīhāsaḥ krīḍā līlā ca narma ca ||
children.translated_text: Keli, drava, parīhāsa, krīḍā, līlā, and narma denote play, sport, or joking.

children.text: devanaṃ kūrdanaṃ khelā lalanaṃ varkaro 'pi ca
children.translated_text: Devana, kūrdana, khelā, lalana, and varkara are also terms for play or amusement.

children.text: vaptā ca janakastāto bījī janayitā pitā ||
children.translated_text: Vaptṛ, janaka, tāta, bījī, janayitṛ, and pitṛ denote a father.
His father is the pitāmaha, the paternal grandfather; that father's father is the prapitāmaha.
For the mother's father and the rest the same pattern applies; mātā, ambā, jananī, and prasū denote a mother.

children.text: savitrī janayitrī ca kṛmilā tu bahuprasūḥ
children.translated_text: Savitrī and janayitrī are also mother terms; kṛmilā denotes a woman who has borne many children.

children.text: dhātrī tu syādupamātā vīramātā tu vīrasūḥ ||
children.translated_text: Dhātrī is an upamātā, a foster-mother or nurse; vīramātā and vīrasū denote the mother of a hero.
Śvaśrū is the mother of one's husband or wife, and śvaśura is the father of either of them.
Pitaraḥ are the ancestors in the father's line; in the mother's family they are the mātāmahas.

children.text: pitarau mātāpitarau mātarapitarau pitā ca mātā ca
children.translated_text: Pitarau, mātāpitarau, and mātarapitarau all denote the two parents, father and mother.

children.text: śvaśrūśvaśurau śvaśurau putrau putraśca duhitā ca ||
children.translated_text: Śvaśrū and śvaśura are the parents-in-law; putrau can mean a son and a daughter.

children.text: bhrātā ca bhaginī cāpi bhrātarāvatha bāndhavaḥ
children.translated_text: Bhrātarau can mean a brother and a sister; now come words for relatives.

children.text: svo jñātiḥ svajano bandhuḥ sagotraśca nijaḥ punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sva, jñāti, svajana, bandhu, sagotra, and again nija mean a kinsman or one's own relative.
Ātmīya, sva, and svakīya mean one's own; sapiṇḍas are also called sanābhaya.
Tṛtīyāprakṛti, paṇḍa, ṣaṇḍha, klība, and napuṃsaka are terms for a neuter or eunuch.
Indriyāyatana, aṅga, vigraha, kṣetra, gātra, tanu, bhū, ghana, and tanū denote the body or embodied form.
Mūrtimat, karaṇa, kāya, mūrti, vera, saṃhanana, deha, and saṃcara are further words for the body.

children.text: ghano bandhaḥ puraṃ piṇḍo vapuḥ pudgalavarṣmaṇī
children.translated_text: Ghana, bandha, pura, piṇḍa, vapuḥ, pudgala, varṣman,
and kalevara are words for this body; when it is lifeless, it is kuṇapa or śava, a corpse.
Mṛtaka means a dead body; ruṇḍa and kabandha denote a headless trunk, especially one still associated with action.

children.text: vayāṃsi tu daśāḥ prāyāḥ sāmudraṃ dehalakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: Vayas, daśā, and prāya denote ages or stages of life; sāmudra is the science of bodily marks.
Pratīka, aṅga, avayava, and apaghana also denote one part or member.
Uttamāṅga, śiras, mūrdhan, mauli, mastaka, and muṇḍaka are names for the head.
Varāṅga, karaṇatrāṇa, śīrṣa, and mastika are also words for the head.
The hair that grows from it is called keśa, tīrthavāka, cikura, kuntala, and kaca.

children.text: vālāḥ syustatparāḥ pāśo racanā bhāra uccayaḥ
children.translated_text: Vāla too means hair; pāśa, racanā, bhāra, and uccaya denote a mass or arrangement of hair.
Hasta, pakṣa, and kalāpa are words expressing an abundance or cluster of hair.
Alaka, karkarāla, khaṃkhara, and cūrṇakuntala denote a curling lock of hair.

children.text: sa tu bhāle bhramarakaḥ kurulo bhramarālakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When such a curl is on the forehead, it is called bhramaraka, kurula, or bhramarālaka.
Dhamilla means tied-up hair; kabarī is a particular coiffure or arrangement of the hair.
Veṇī and praveṇī mean a braid; śīrṣaṇya and śirasya are used of clear or well-kept head-hair.

children.text: keśeṣu vartma sīmantaḥ palitaṃ pāṇḍuraḥ kacaḥ
children.translated_text: A parting in the hair is vartman or sīmanta; grey hair is palita, a pale or white hair.

children.text: cūḍā keśī keśapāśī śikhā śikhaṇḍikā samāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Cūḍā, keśī, keśapāśī, śikhā, and śikhaṇḍikā are equivalent terms for a topknot or crest of hair.
For children that lock is called kākapakṣa, śikhaṇḍaka, or śikhāṇḍaka.
Tuṇḍa, āsya, mukha, vaktra, lapana, vadana, and ānana are words for the mouth or face.
Bhāla, godhi, alika, alīka, and lalāṭa are words for the forehead; śruti and śravas are terms for the ear or hearing.
Śabdādhiṣṭhāna, paiñjūṣa, mahānāda, and dhvanigraha are further names connected with the ear as the seat of sound.

children.text: karṇaḥ śrotraṃ śravaṇaṃ ca veṣṭanaṃ karṇaśaṣkulī
children.translated_text: Karṇa, śrotra, śravaṇa, veṣṭana, and karṇaśaṣkulī are names for the ear.
The ear-lobe is pāli or karṇalatikā; śaṅkha is the temple, the space between the forehead and the ear.
Cakṣus, akṣi, īkṣaṇa, netra, nayana, dṛṣṭi, and ambaka are words for the eye.

children.text: locanaṃ darśanaṃ dṛkca tattārā tu kanīnikā ||
children.translated_text: Locana, darśana, and dṛk are also words for the eye; its tārā, the pupil, is called kanīnikā.

children.text: vāmaṃ tu nayanaṃ saumyaṃ bhānavīyaṃ tu dakṣiṇam
children.translated_text: The left eye is called saumya, moon-like; the right eye is called bhānavīya, sun-like.
An inauspicious eye is akṣaṇya or anakṣi; īkṣaṇa and niśāmana denote seeing.
Nibhālana, niśamana, nidhyāna, and avalokana are words for looking or beholding.
Darśana, dyotana, and nirvarṇana also denote seeing; next, ardhavīkṣaṇa means a half-glance.
Apāṅgadarśana, kākṣa, kaṭākṣa, and akṣivikūṇita denote a sidelong glance.
Unmīlana and unmeṣa mean opening the eyes, while nimeṣa and nimīlana mean closing them.
The outer ends of the eyes are apāṅgas; above them is the row of hairs called the brow.
A change of the brow in anger is a frown, called bhrūkuṭi and related forms.
Kūrca and kūrpa denote the space between the brows; pakṣman is the hair of the eye, the eyelash.

children.text: gandhajñā nāsikā nāsā ghrāṇaṃ ghoṇā vikūṇikā ||
children.translated_text: Gandhajñā, nāsikā, nāsā, ghrāṇa, ghoṇā, and vikūṇikā are words for the nose or organ of smell.
Nakra, narkuṭaka, and śiṅghinī are nasal terms; oṣṭha, adhara, and radacchada mean the lip.

children.text: dantavastraṃ ca tatprāntau sṛkkaṇī asikaṃ tvadhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Dantavastra is another word for the lip; its two ends are sṛkkaṇī, and below is the asika.
Below the asikā is the cibuka, the chin; beyond the sṛkkaṇa is the galla.
Beyond the galla is the kapola, the cheek; beyond the kapola is the gaṇḍa.

children.text: tato hanuḥ śmaśru kūrcamāsyaloma ca māsurī
children.translated_text: After that is the hanu, the jaw; śmaśru, kūrca, āsyaloman, and māsurī denote beard or facial hair.

children.text: dāḍhikā daṃṣṭrikā dāḍhā daṃṣṭrā jambho dvijā radāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Dāḍhikā, daṃṣṭrikā, dāḍhā, and daṃṣṭrā are terms for fangs or large teeth; jambha, dvija, and rada denote teeth.
Radana, daśana, danta, daṃśa, khādana, and mallaka are also words for teeth.
The two middle teeth in the upper row are sometimes called the rājadantau, the royal teeth.

children.text: rasajñā rasanā jihvā lolā tālu tu kākudam
children.translated_text: Rasajñā, rasanā, jihvā, and lolā are words for the tongue; tālu and kākuda mean the palate.
Sudhāsravā, ghaṇṭikā, lambikā, and galaśuṇḍikā are names for the uvula.
Kaṃdharā, dhamani, grīvā, śirodhi, and śirodharā are names for the neck.
When the neck has three lines it is called kambugrīvā; vaṭu, ghāṭā, and kṛkāṭikā are terms connected with the nape.
Kṛka is the middle of the neck; the two sides of the neck are called kuka and vītana.
The neck-veins in front are called nīlā; behind they are manyā and kalambikā.
Gala, nigaraṇa, and kaṇṭha mean the throat; kākalaka is its projecting knot.
Aṃsa, bhujaśiras, and skandha are names for the shoulder; jatru is the joint where the chest and shoulder meet.
Bhuja, bāhu, praveṣṭa, dor, and bāhā are words for the arm; then comes the bhujakoṭara.
Bhujakoṭara, dormūla, khaṇḍikā, and kakṣā denote the armpit; below the two arms is the side, pārśva.
Kaphoṇi, kaphaṇi, and kūrpara denote the middle of the arm, the elbow.
Below that, as far as the wrist, is the prakoṣṭha, also called kalācikā, the forearm.
Pragaṇḍa is the upper arm up to the elbow; the five-branched hand is called śaya or śama.

children.text: hastaḥ pāṇiḥ karasyādau maṇibandho maṇiśca saḥ ||
children.translated_text: Hasta, pāṇi, and kara are words for the hand; at the beginning of the hand is the wrist, maṇibandha or maṇi.
Karabha is the part of the hand up to the little finger; karaśākhā and aṅgulī alike mean finger.
Aṅguri and aṅgula are also words for a finger; aṅguṣṭha is the thumb, and tarjanī is the pradeśinī, the index finger.

children.text: jyeṣṭhā tu madhyamā madhyā sāvitrī syādanāmikā
children.translated_text: Jyeṣṭhā, madhyamā, and madhyā denote the middle finger; sāvitrī is the anāmikā, the ring finger.
Kanīnikā and kaniṣṭhā denote the little finger; avahasta is the back of the hand.
Kāmāṅkuśa, mahārāja, karaja, nakhara, and nakha are words for the nail.
Karaśūka, bhujākaṇṭa, punarbhava, and punarnava are further terms for the nail.
When the thumb is extended together with the index finger and the following fingers,
the measures are called prādeśa, tāla, gokarṇa, and vitasti respectively.
A hand with its fingers spread out is called capeṭa, pratala, or tala.
Prahasta, tālika, and tāla are also such open-hand terms; when the two hands are joined it is siṃhatāla.
A hand with the fingers compressed together is a muṣṭi, also called musti or mucuṭi.
Saṃgrāha and ardhamuṣṭi mean a half-fist; khaṭaka is again a bent or curved hand.
An outstretched hand is prasṛti; when the two hands are joined, it is añjali.
For water held or poured out, the terms are prasṛta, jalādhāra, gaṇḍūṣa, śruluka, and calu.
A hasta, as a measure, extends from the tip of the middle finger to the elbow.
The same measure with the fist closed is ratni; without the little finger it is aratni.
Vyāma, vyāyāma, and nyagrodha denote the two arms stretched out sideways.
When the arms and hands are raised upward, the man's measure is called pauruṣa.
Measures ending at the knee and the like, called daghna measures, are reckoned according to each such height.

children.text: rīḍhakaḥ pṛṣṭhavaṃśaḥ syātpṛṣṭhaṃ tu caramaṃ tanoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Rīḍhaka and pṛṣṭhavaṃśa denote the backbone; pṛṣṭha is the rear part of the body.
The front or lap region is called upastha, aṅka, kroḍa, and utsaṅga.
Koḍora is the region of the heart; vakṣas, vatsas, and bhujāntara denote the chest, the space between the arms.
Hṛd and hṛdaya denote the heart between the breasts; the two breasts are kuca and payodhara.
Uroja also denotes the breasts; the nipple is cūcuka, stanavṛnta, śikhā, or mukha.
Tunda, tundi, garbha, kukṣi, picaṇḍa, jaṭhara, and udara denote the belly or abdomen.
Kālakhaṇḍa, kālakhañja, kāleya, kālaka, and yakṛt denote the liver.

children.text: dakṣiṇe tilakaṃ kloma vāme tu raktaphenajaḥ
children.translated_text: On the right is the organ called tilaka or kloman; on the left is the blood-foam-born organ.

children.text: puṣpasaḥ syādatha plīhā gulmo 'traṃ tu purītati ||
children.translated_text: That organ is called puṣpasa; next, plīhā denotes the spleen, while gulma, āntra, and purītati denote the entrails.
Romāvalī and romalatā denote a line of hair; nābhi and tundakūpikā denote the navel.
Below the navel is the mūtrapuṭa; vasti and mūtrāśaya also denote the urinary bladder.
Avalagna, vilagna, madhyama, kaṭa, and kaṭi denote the waist or middle.
Śroṇi, kalatra, kaṭīra, kāñcīpada, and kakadmatī are terms for the hips or loins.
Nitamba and āroha denote the rear of a woman's hips; jaghana denotes the front.
Trika is the part below the spine; the hollows at its two sides are kukundaras.

children.text: pūtau sphijau kaṭiprothau varāṅgaṃ tu cyutirbuliḥ
children.translated_text: Pūta, sphij, and kaṭiprotha denote the buttocks; varāṅga, cyuti, and buli denote the private part.
Bhaga, apatyapatha, yoni, smaramandira, and kūpikā denote the female generative organ.
This is the female mark; next, the male mark is mehana, śepa, and śepas.

children.text: śiśnaṃ meḍhraḥ kāmalatā liṅgaṃ ca dvayamapyadaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Śiśna, meḍhra, kāmalatā, and liṅga are also used, and liṅga can refer to either sex.
Guhya, prajanana, and upastha denote the genitals; the middle of the private part is gula or maṇi.
Sīvanī is the seam-like line below it; aṇḍa, pela, and maṇḍaka denote the testicle.
Muṣka, aṇḍakoṣa, and vṛṣaṇa denote the scrotal or testicular part; apāna, pāyu, guda, and cyuti denote the anus.
Adhomarma and śakṛddvāra are also terms for the anus, as are tribalīka and kavulī.
Viṭapa, also called mahāvījya, is the region between the scrotum and the groin.
Ūrusaṃdhi and vaṅkṣaṇa denote the groin; sakthi and ūru denote the thigh, and its joint is parvan.
Jānu, nalakīla, and aṣṭhīvat denote the knee; its back part is mandira.
Kapolī is the front part; jaṅghā, prasṛtā, and nalakinī denote the lower leg.
Pratijaṅghā and agrajaṅghā denote the shin; piṇḍikā and picaṇḍikā denote the calf.
Gulpha, caraṇagranthi, ghuṭika, ghuṇṭaka, and puṭa denote the ankle.
Caraṇa, kramaṇa, pāda, pada, aṅghri, calana, and krama denote the foot.
Pādamūla and gohira denote the root or sole of the foot; pārṣṇi is the heel below the ankles.
Pādāgra and prapada denote the front of the foot; kṣipra is the space between the big toe and the toe beside it.
Kūrca lies above the kṣipra; aṅghriskandha and kūrcaśiras are equivalent terms.

children.text: talahṛdayaṃ tu talaṃ madhye pādatalasya tat
children.translated_text: Talahṛdaya, or simply tala, is the middle of the sole of the foot.
Tilaka, kālaka, piplu, jaḍula, and tilakālaka denote a mole or dark mark.
The <s>dhātus</s> (bodily constituents) are rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
They are exactly seven, though for some they are ten when hair, skin, and sinews are included.
Rasa is the essence of food, produced by digestive fire; ṣaḍrasa and āsava are also terms for it.
It is the constituent that makes blood and is also called <s>Ātreya</s>, ghana, mūla, and mahāpara.
Rakta, rudhira, āgneya, visra, and tejobhava denote blood, which arises from rasa.
Śoṇita, lohita, asṛj, <s>Vāsiṣṭha</s>, prāṇada, and asura are further terms for blood.
Kṣataja and māṃsakāryasra are also blood terms; māṃsa, palala, and jāṅgala denote flesh.
Kravya, <s>Kāśyapa</s>, taras, and āmiṣa are terms for flesh, which is produced from blood and heat.
Piśita, kīna, and pala also denote flesh, the producer of fat; peśīs are its strip-like bands.

children.text: vukkā hṛddhṛdayaṃ vṛkkā surasaṃ ca tadagrimam ||
children.translated_text: Vukkā and vṛkkā denote the kidneys, hṛd and hṛdaya the heart, and surasa the part in front of it.
Dried flesh is called vallūra and uttama; pūya and dūṣya are equivalent terms for pus.
Medas, asthikṛt, vapā, <s>Gautama</s>, and vasā denote fat, born from flesh and heat.
Goda is the oil of the head; mastiṣka and mastuluṅgaka denote the brain.
Asthi, kulya, and <s>Bhāradvāja</s> denote bone, produced from fat and heat and producing marrow.
Māṃsapitta, śvadayita, karkara, and dehadhāraka are further terms for bone.
Kīkasa and sāra denote bone born from fat; karoṭi is the bone of the head.
Kapāla and karpara are equivalent; kaśerukā is a bone of the back, a vertebra.
Nalaka denotes a limb-bone; vaṅkri and parśuka denote a rib, the bone of the side.
Karaṅka, kaṅkāla, and asthipañjara denote the skeleton, the bones of the body.
Majjā and <s>Kauśika</s> denote marrow, produced from the unctuous part of bone and making semen.

children.text: śukraṃ reto balaṃ vīryaṃ bījaṃ majjasamudbhavam
children.translated_text: Śukra, retas, bala, vīrya, and bīja denote semen, which arises from marrow.
It is born of pleasure, is masculinity and the generative faculty, and is free of waste.
Pauruṣa and pradhānadhātu are further terms for it; loma, roma, and tanūruha denote body hair.
Tvak, chavi, chādanī, kṛtti, carma, ajina, and asṛgdhara denote the skin.
Vasnasā, snasā, and snāyu denote sinew; nāḍī, dhamanī, and śirā denote bodily vessels.
Kaṇḍarā is a great sinew or tendon; mala and kiṭṭa denote waste produced from these tissues.

children.text: dūṣīkā dūṣikā jaihvaṃ kulukaṃ pippikā punaḥ
children.translated_text: Dūṣīkā and dūṣikā denote ocular impurity; kuluka is tongue impurity, and pippikā denotes dental impurity.

children.text: dantyaṃ kārṇaṃ tu piñjūṣaḥ śiṅghāṇo ghrāṇasaṃbhavam ||
children.translated_text: Piñjūṣa is ear impurity, and śiṅghāṇa is the discharge produced from the nose.
Sṛṇīkā, syandinī, lālā, āsyāsava, and kaphakūrcikā denote saliva or mucus of the mouth.

children.text: mūtraṃ bastimalaṃ mehaḥ prasrāvo nṛjalaṃ sravaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Mūtra, bastimala, meha, prasrāva, nṛjala, and srava denote urine.
Puṣpikā is genital impurity; viṭ, viṣṭhā, avaskara, and śakṛt denote feces.
Gūtha, purīṣa, śamala, uccāra, varcaska, and varcas are further terms for feces.
Veṣa, nepathya, ākalpa, parikarma, and aṅgasaṃskriyā denote dress, costume, and bodily preparation.
Udvartana, utsādana, aṅgarāga, and vilepana denote rubbing, massage, and cosmetic unguent.
Carcikya, samālabhana, and carcā denote anointing; maṇḍana means adornment.
Prasādhana and pratikarma mean adornment; mārṣṭi, mārjana, and mṛjā mean cleansing or polishing.
Vāsayoga is fragrant powder, and when it is ground into a paste it is called paṭavāsaka.
The preparation made with perfumes, garlands, and the like is called adhivāsana, perfuming or consecrating by scent.
Nirveśa and upabhoga mean enjoyment or use; snāna, savana, and āplava mean bathing.
The ingredients include liquids of camphor, aguru, kola, musk, and sandalwood.
When they are mixed, the paste is yakṣakardama; varti is an unguent applied to the body.
It may also be made in four equal parts from sandalwood, aguru, musk, and saffron.
Aguru is also called agaru, rājārha, loha, kṛmija, and vaṃśika.
Anāryaja, joṅgika, maṅgalya, and malligandhi are also names for it.
Kālāguru is called kālatuṇḍa; śrīkhaṇḍa and rohaṇadruma are names of sandalwood.
Gandhasāra, malayaja, candana, and haricandana likewise denote sandalwood.
Tailaparṇika and gośīrṣa are sandalwood varieties; patrāṅga is red sandalwood.
Kucandana, tāmrasāra, rañjana, and tilaparṇikā are also names for red sandalwood.
Jātikośa and jātiphala are mace and nutmeg; karpūra is himavālukā, camphor.
Ghanasāra, sitābhra, and candra are further names for camphor; next comes the substance born from the deer's navel.
Mṛganābhi, mṛgamada, kastūrī, and gandhadhūli all mean musk.
Kaśmīrajanma, ghusṛṇa, varṇa, and lohitacandana are names for saffron or red fragrant dye.
Vālhīka, kuṅkuma, vahniśikha, kāleya, and jāguḍa are names for the same saffron substance.
Saṃkoca, piśuna, rakta, dhīra, and pītanadīpana are additional names for it.
Lavaṅga, the clove, is called devakusuma and śrīsaṃjña; next, kolaka is treated.
Kakkolaka and kośaphala are names for kolaka, while kālīyaka is called jāpaka.
Yakṣadhūpa, bahurūpa, sālaveṣṭa, and agnivallabha are names for fragrant resin-incense.
Sarjamaṇi, sarjarasa, rāla, and sarvarasa are also names for it.
Dhūpa, incense, is either tree-derived or artificial; turuṣka and silhapiṇḍaka are incense-resin terms.
Pāyasa, vṛkṣadhūpa, śrīvāsa, and saraladrava denote tree-derived incense resin.
Incense that goes from one place to another as scent is called gandhapiśācikā.
Sthāsaka denotes a hand mirror; alaṃkāra is ornament, also called bhūṣaṇa.
Pariṣkāra and ābharaṇa also mean ornament; cūḍāmaṇi and śiromaṇi are crest-jewels.
Nāyaka and tarala denote the central gem within a necklace; mukuṭa is next.
Mukuṭa, mauli, kirīṭa, koṭīra, and uṣṇīṣa are head-dresses or crowns; puṣpadāma is a flower-wreath.
A flower garland on the head is mālya, mālā, or sraj; svagarbhaka is one set amid the hair.
Prabhraṣṭaka is one hanging from the topknot; lalāmaka is one placed at the front.
Vaikakṣa is worn crosswise on the chest; prālamba is what hangs straight down.

children.text: saṃdarbho racanā gumpha: sranthanaṃ manthanaṃ samāḥ
children.translated_text: Saṃdarbha, racanā, gumpha, sranthana, and manthana are equivalent terms for arranging or stringing.
Tilaka, tamālapatra, citrapuṇḍra, and viśeṣaka are marks painted on the forehead.
Āpīḍa, śekhara, uttaṃsa, and vataṃsa are wreaths or ornaments for the head.
The last two can also mean ear-ornaments; patralekhā is a decoration made from leaf.
Bhaṅgi, vallī, latāṅgulī, pattrapāśyā, and lalāṭikā are decorative patterns or forehead ornaments.
Vālapāśyā, pāritathyā, and karṇikā denote ornaments of the ear.
Tāḍaṅka is tāḍapattra; kuṇḍala and karṇaveṣṭaka are earrings.
Utkṣiptikā is an ear ornament; bālīkā is worn behind the ear.
Graiveyaka is a neck ornament; a hanging one is lalambikā.
Prālambikā is made of gold, while an uraḥsūtrikā is made with pearls.
A hāra is a hanging string of pearls; srak, kalāpa, āvalī, and latā are strings or garlands.
A devacchanda necklace has one hundred and eight pearls, while an indracchanda has a thousand.
The vijayacchanda is half of that; a hāra, however, has one hundred and eight.
Half of this is a raśmikalāpa; an ardhamāṇava has twelve.
An ardhaguccha is twice twelve; hāraphala and latā are counted among the necklace varieties.
An ardhahāra has sixty-four; guccha, māṇava, and mandara are further varieties.
Gostana, gopuccha, and vardhamāna are arranged successively by halves.
These are the distinctions of necklace-strands; ekāvalī and ekayaṣṭikā mean a single strand.
Kaṇṭhikā is another neck ornament; a nakṣatramālā has pearls equal to the number of the lunar mansions.
Keyūra and aṅgada are arm ornaments; now the ornaments of the hand are given.
Kaṭaka, valaya, pārihārya, āvāpa, and kaṅkaṇa are bracelets.
Hastasūtra and pratisara are wrist-threads; ūrmikā is a finger-ring, an aṅgulīyaka.
When that ring bears letters it is an aṅgulimudrā; a waist-string is a mekhalā.

children.text: kalāpo raśanā sā rasanaṃ kāñcī ca saptakī ||
children.translated_text: Kalāpa and raśanā are the same girdle; rasana, kāñcī, and saptakī are also its names.
When it is at a man's waist it is śṛṅkhala; a kiṃkiṇī is a small bell.
Nūpura and tulākoṭi are anklets; kaṭaka and aṅgada may also denote ornaments of the feet.
Mañjīra, haṃsaka, and śiñjinī are anklets; aṃśuka, vastra, and ambara mean cloth or garment.
Sicaya, vasana, cīra, ācchāda, sicela, and vāsas are also words for garment.
Paṭa and prota are cloth; añcala is its end, and varti, vasti, and daśā are its borders or fringes.
Pattrorṇa is washed silk; uṣṇīṣa is a head-wrapping, a turban.
A pair of washed garments is called udgamanīya.
Cloth is fourfold because it comes from bark, fruit, worms, or hair.
The divisions include kṣauma, kārpāsa, kauśeya, and rāṅkava.

children.text: kṣaumaṃ dukūlaṃ dugūlaṃ syātkārpāsaṃ tu bādaram ||
children.translated_text: Kṣauma, dukūla, and dugūla are linen or fine cloth; kārpāsa, also called bādara, is cotton.
Kauśeya is made from a silkworm's cocoon; rāṅkava is made from animal hair.
Kambala, ūrṇāyu, āvika, aurabhra, and rallaka denote woolen cloth or blankets.
New cloth is anāhata; tantraka and niṣpravāṇi are also terms for unworn cloth.
Pracchādana, prāvaraṇa, saṃvyāna, and uttarīyaka are covering or upper garments.
Vaikakṣa, prāvāra, uttarāsaṅga, and bṛhatikā are also upper wraps.
Varāśi is a coarse śāṭa cloth; paridhāna is the lower garment.
Antarīya, nivasana, and upasaṃvyāna also denote the lower garment.
The knot of that garment is uccaya or nīvī; a woman's half-thigh cloth is specified next.
Caṇḍātaka and calanaka denote it; calanī is the corresponding feminine form.
Cola, kañculikā, kūrpāsaka, and aṅgikā are names for a bodice or jacket, a kañcuka.
Śāṭī and coṭī are garments; nīśāra is a cloth that wards off cold, wind, and heat.
Kacchā, kacchāṭikā, and kakṣā denote the rear end of a lower garment.
Kakṣāpaṭa is a kaupīna, a loincloth; naktāka and karpaṭa are equivalent terms.
Nicola is a covering cloth, and nicula denotes an upper covering.
At festivals, when friends forcibly pull something away and take it,
that garment, garland, or the like is called pūrṇapātra, and also pūrṇānaka.
That which reaches down as far as the forepart of the foot is called āprapadīna.
Cīvara is a monk's saṃghāṭī robe; an old garment is called paṭaccara.
Śāṇī and goṇī denote a cloth full of holes; jalārdrā denotes a wet garment.
Paryastikā, parikara, paryaṅka, and avasakthikā are equivalent terms for a wrapping or support about the seated body.
For a kutha coverlet or rug, varṇaparistoma, praveṇī, and navatāstara are synonyms.
Apaṭī is a kāṇḍapaṭa; pratisīrā and javanī are also terms for a curtain.
Tiraskariṇī denotes a screen; ulloca, vitāna, and kadaka are words for an awning or canopy.
Candrodaya denotes a thick cloth-covering, and keṇikā is also a cloth hut or tent.
Saṃstara and srastara are equivalent words for a spread layer or bedding arranged in a mass.

children.text: talpaṃ śayyā śayanīyaṃ śayanaṃ talinaṃ ca tat ||
children.translated_text: Talpa, śayyā, śayanīya, śayana, and talina all denote a bed.
Mañca, mañcaka, paryaṅka, and palyaṅka are equivalent to khaṭvā, a bedstead or couch.
Ucchīrṣaka, upādhāna, varha, upāla, and patadgraha are words for a pillow or head-rest.
Mukura, ātmadarśa, and ādarśa are names for a darpaṇa, a mirror.
Vetrāsana, āsandī, viṣṭara, pīṭha, and āsana are words for a seat.
Kasipu is used for food and covering; auśira denotes a bed and a seat.
Lākṣā, lac, is also called drumāmaya, rākṣā, raṅgamātā, and palaṃkaṣā.

children.text: jatu kṣataghnā kṛmijā yāvālaktau tu tadrasaḥ
children.translated_text: Jatu, kṣataghnā, and kṛmijā are further names for it; yāva and alakta denote its red extract.
Añjana and kajjala mean collyrium or lamp-black; dīpa, pradīpa, and kajjaladhvaja are names for a lamp.
Snehapriya, gṛhamaṇi, daśākarṣa, and daśendhana are further names for a lamp.
Vyajana and tālavṛnta denote a fan; when made with deer-skin, it is called dhavitra.
Ālāvarta is a fold or twist of cloth; kaṅkata denotes a comb for arranging the hair.
Prasādhana too is a grooming implement; next, among children's toys, there are guḍa and giri.
Giriyaka and giriguḍa are equivalent, and kanduka and genduka both mean a ball.
Rājā, rāṭ, pṛthivīśa, kramadhyalokeśa, and bhūbhṛt are terms for a king.
Mahīkṣit, pārthiva, mūrdhābhiṣikta, bhūpa, prajānṛpa, and nṛpa are also words for a king.

children.text: madhyamo maṇḍalādhīśaḥ sa samrāṭ śāsti yo nṛpān ||
children.translated_text: The ruler of a maṇḍala is called madhyama or maṇḍalādhīśa; one who commands other kings is a samrāṭ.
He who is lord of the whole circle of realms and who has achieved the rājasūya consecration
is called a cakravartin or sārvabhauma; such rulers are twelve in <s>Bhārata</s>.
Among them, <s>Bharata</s> was the son of <s>Ṛṣabha</s>, and <s>Sagara</s> was the son of <s>Sumitra</s>.
<s>Maghavan</s>, called <s>Vaijayiratha</s>, was the son of king <s>Aśvasena</s>.
Then come <s>Sanatkumāra</s>, and the Jinas <s>Śānti</s>, <s>Kunthu</s>, and <s>Ara</s>.
<s>Subhūma</s> was of the <s>Kārtavīrya</s> line, and <s>Padma</s> was the son of <s>Padmottara</s>.
<s>Hariṣeṇa</s> was the son of <s>Hari</s>, and <s>Jaya</s> was the son of <s>Vijaya</s>.
<s>Brahmadatta</s> was the son of <s>Brahmā</s>; all these too were born in the <s>Ikṣvāku</s> lineage.
<s>Tripṛṣṭha</s> was the son of <s>Prajāpati</s>; next, <s>Dvipṛṣṭha</s> was born from <s>Brahmā</s>.
<s>Svayaṃbhū</s> was the son of <s>Rudra</s>, and <s>Puruṣottama</s> was born from <s>Soma</s>.
<s>Puruṣasiṃha</s> was connected with <s>Śiva</s>; then, born from <s>Mahāśiras</s>,
there is <s>Puruṣapuṇḍarīka</s>, and <s>Datta</s> was the son of <s>Agnisiṃha</s>.
<s>Nārāyaṇa</s> was <s>Dāśarathi</s>, while <s>Kṛṣṇa</s> was the son of <s>Vasudeva</s>.

children.text: vāsudevā amī kṛṣṇā nava śuklā balāstvamī ||
children.translated_text: These are the nine dark <s>Vāsudevas</s>; the white <s>Balas</s> are these:
<s>Acala</s>, <s>Vijaya</s>, <s>Bhadra</s>, <s>Suprabha</s>, and <s>Sudarśana</s>,
<s>Ānanda</s>, <s>Nandana</s>, <s>Padma</s>, and <s>Rāma</s>; these others are the enemies of the <s>Viṣṇus</s>.
<s>Aśvagrīva</s>, <s>Tāraka</s>, <s>Meraka</s>, and <s>Madhura</s>,
<s>Niśumbha</s>, <s>Bali</s>, <s>Prahlāda</s>, the lord of <s>Laṅkā</s>, and the lord of <s>Magadha</s>.

children.text: jinaiḥ saha triṣaṣṭiḥ syuḥ śalākāpuruṣā amī
children.translated_text: Together with the Jinas, these are the sixty-three <s>śalākāpuruṣas</s>.
<s>Ādirāja</s> is <s>Pṛthu</s>, son of <s>Vena</s>; <s>Māndhātṛ</s> was the son of <s>Yuvanāśva</s>.
<s>Dhundhumāra</s> is <s>Kuvalāśva</s>; <s>Hariścandra</s> was the son of <s>Triśaṅku</s>.
<s>Purūravas</s>, descendant of <s>Budha</s>, is <s>Aila</s>, and he is the lover of <s>Urvaśī</s>.
<s>Bharata</s>, son of <s>Duṣyanta</s>, is <s>Sarvadamana</s>, the son of <s>Śakuntalā</s>.
The <s>Haihaya</s> <s>Kārtavīrya</s> is <s>Arjuna</s>, bearer of a thousand arms.
<s>Rāma</s>, the son of <s>Kauśalyā</s> and descendant of <s>Daśaratha</s>, has as his beloved
<s>Vaidehī</s>, <s>Maithilī</s>, <s>Sītā</s>, <s>Jānakī</s>, the daughter of the Earth.
The two sons of <s>Rāma</s> are <s>Kuśa</s> and <s>Lava</s>; in one expression they are <s>Kuśīlava</s>.
<s>Saumitri</s> is <s>Lakṣmaṇa</s>; <s>Vālī</s> or <s>Vālin</s> is the son of <s>Indra</s>.
<s>Sugrīva</s> is the son of <s>Āditya</s>; <s>Hanumān</s> is called <s>Vajrakaṅkaṭa</s>.
<s>Māruti</s>, son of <s>Kesari</s>, <s>Āñjaneya</s>, and <s>Arjunadhvaja</s> are names of <s>Hanumān</s>.
The <s>Paulastya</s> is <s>Rāvaṇa</s>, the rākṣasa, lord of <s>Laṅkā</s>, and ten-necked one.
<s>Rāvaṇi</s>, <s>Śakrajit</s>, <s>Meghanāda</s>, and son of <s>Mandodarī</s> are names of <s>Indrajit</s>.
<s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s> is <s>Ajātaśatru</s>, enemy of <s>Śalya</s>, and son of <s>Dharma</s>.
<s>Kaṅka</s> and <s>Ājamīḍha</s> are also his names; <s>Bhīma</s> is <s>Marutputra</s> and <s>Vṛkodara</s>.
He is the destroyer of <s>Kirmīra</s>, <s>Kīcaka</s>, <s>Baka</s>, and <s>Hiḍamba</s>.
<s>Arjuna</s>, <s>Phālguna</s>, <s>Pārtha</s>, <s>Savyasācī</s>, and <s>Dhanaṃjaya</s> are names of <s>Arjuna</s>.
<s>Rādhāvedhī</s>, <s>Kirīṭin</s>, <s>Aindri</s>, <s>Jiṣṇu</s>, <s>Śvetahaya</s>, and <s>Nara</s> are further names of him.
<s>Bṛhannala</s>, <s>Guḍākeśa</s>, <s>Subhadreśa</s>, and <s>Kapidhvaja</s> are further names of <s>Arjuna</s>.
<s>Bībhatsa</s> and <s>Karṇajit</s> are his names; his bow is <s>Gāṇḍīva</s> or <s>Gāṇḍiva</s>.
<s>Pāñcālī</s>, <s>Draupadī</s>, <s>Kṛṣṇā</s>, <s>Sairaṃdhrī</s>, and <s>Nityayauvanā</s> are names of <s>Draupadī</s>.
<s>Vedijā</s> and <s>Yājñasenī</s> are also her names; <s>Karṇa</s> is lord of <s>Campā</s> and king of <s>Aṅga</s>.
<s>Rādhāsuta</s> and <s>Arkatanaya</s> are names of <s>Karṇa</s>; his bow is <s>Kālapṛṣṭha</s>.
<s>Śreṇika</s> is <s>Bhaṃbhāsāra</s>, and <s>Hāla</s> is <s>Sātavāhana</s>.
<s>Kumārapāla</s> is the <s>Caulukya</s> king, a royal sage and supreme devotee of the Arhats.
He released the property of the dead, was righteous-souled, and warded off the calamity of pestilence.
Rājabījī and rājavaṃśya mean one of royal seed or lineage; bīja and vaṃśya denote a descendant.
The elements of sovereignty are the lord, minister, ally, treasury, territory, fortress, and army.
Prakṛtis are the constituents of a kingdom, and śreṇis are also the guilds or groups of townsmen.
Tantra is concern for one's own realm, while āvāpa is concern about the enemy.
Parispanda, parikara, parivāra, and parigraha are terms for an attendant apparatus or retinue.
Paricchada and paribarha too denote that same equipment.
Rājaśayyā and mahāśayyā mean a royal bed; bhadrāsana and nṛpāsana mean a royal seat.
A golden royal seat is called siṃhāsana; chatra means a parasol that wards off the sun.
Cāmara, bālavyajana, romaguccha, and prakīrṇaka are words for a fly-whisk or tail-fan.
Sthagī is a betel casket, while bhṛṅgāra and kanakālukā are ceremonial vessels.
Bhadrakumbha and pūrṇakumbha mean an auspicious full jar; pādapīṭha and padāsana mean a footstool.
Amātya, saciva, mantrī, dhīsakha, and sāmavāyika are words for a minister or counsellor.
Niyogin, karmasaciva, āyukta, and vyāpṛta are also terms for such an appointed official.
The official who examines legal proceedings is called prāḍvivāka or akṣadarśaka.
Mahāmātra denotes a chief officer, while purodhā denotes a purohita, a royal priest.
Sauvastika is another palace official; dvārastha, kṣattā, and dvārapālaka denote a doorkeeper.
Dauvārika, pratīhāra, vetrin, utsāraka, and daṇḍin are terms for doorkeepers, ushers, or staff-bearing guards.
Among guards, anīkastha is a guard; adhyakṣa and adhikṛta are equivalent terms for a superintendent or officer.
Paurogava means superintendent of cooks; sūda, audanika, and guṇa denote a cook.
Bhaktakāra, sūpakāra, sūpārālika, and ballava are also words for a cook or preparer of food.
Bhaurika denotes a superintendent of gold, while naiṣkika denotes a superintendent of silver.
Sthānika means superintendent of a station, and śaulkika means superintendent of tolls.
Śulka is a toll payable at a ferry, landing, or the like; dhārmika means superintendent of justice or dharma.
Dharmādhikaraṇī is a court of law; adhikarmika means superintendent of a market.
Senānī and daṇḍanāyaka are commanders of the fourfold army.
Sthāyuka is the officer appointed in a village, and gopa is the officer over many villages.
Antarvaṃśika and avarodhika denote superintendents of the inner apartments.
Śuddhānta, antaḥpura, avarodha, and avarodhana mean the royal inner apartments or harem.
Sauvidalla, kañcukin, sthāpatya, and sauvida are terms for such chamberlains or inner-palace attendants.

children.text: ṣaṇḍhe varṣavaraḥ śatrau pratipakṣaḥ paro ripuḥ
children.translated_text: Varṣavara denotes a eunuch; pratipakṣa, para, and ripu denote an enemy.
Śātrava, pratyavasthātṛ, pratyanīka, abhiyātin, and ari are also enemy terms.

children.text: dasyuḥ sapatno 'sahano vipakṣo dveṣī dviṣanvairyahito jighāṃsuḥ
children.translated_text: Dasyu, sapatna, asahana, vipakṣa, dveṣin, dviṣant, vairya, ahita, and jighāṃsu denote a foe or hostile person.
Durhṛt, para, panthaka, panthin, dviṭ, pratyarthin, amitra, abhimāti, and arāti are further words for an enemy.

children.text: vairaṃ virodho vidveṣo vayasyaḥ savayāḥ suhat
children.translated_text: Vaira, virodha, and vidveṣa mean enmity; vayasya, savayas, and suhṛd denote a friend.

children.text: snigdhaḥ sahacaro mittraṃ sakhā sakhyaṃ tu sauhṛdam ||
