children.translated_text: Snigdha, sahacara, mitra, and sakhā also mean friend; sakhya means friendship or goodwill.
Sauhārda, sāptapadīna, maittra, yajarya, and saṃgata are terms for friendship or alliance.
Ānandana, āpracchana, and sabhājana also denote respectful greeting, inquiry, or honoring.
A king whose territory is immediately adjacent is an enemy; the one beyond him is an ally.
The more distant king is neutral, while a pārṣṇigrāha is one who attacks from the rear.
Anuvṛtti means compliance or anurodha; herika means a secret agent.
Praṇidhi, yathārhavarṇa, avasarpa, and mantravicara are terms for spies or secret agents.
Vārtāyana, spaśa, and cāra are spies; āpta and pratyayita alike mean a trusted person.
A sattrin-spy may be called gṛhapati; a dūta is a bearer of messages.
Saṃdhi, vigraha, yāna, āsana, dvaidha, and āśraya--peace, war, marching, staying, dual policy, and seeking shelter--
are the six policies; the three powers arise from sovereignty, energy, and counsel.
Sāma, dāna, bheda, and daṇḍa are the means of policy; sāma means conciliation or soothing.
Upajāpa is bheda, the sowing of dissension; daṇḍa is force, punishment, or restraint.
Prābhṛta, ḍhaukana, lamba, utkoca, kauśalika, and āmiṣa are terms for gifts, inducements, or bribes.

children.text: upāccāraḥ pradānaṃ dā hāro grāhyāyane api ||
children.translated_text: Upāccāra, pradāna, dā, hāra, and grāhyāyana also denote giving or a present.
Māyā, upekṣā, and indrajāla are these three lesser expedients.
Hunting, dice, women, drinking, harsh speech, and misuse of wealth,
together with harsh punishment, make up the seven vices that are to be avoided.

children.text: pauruṣaṃ vikramaḥ śauryaṃ śauṭīryaṃ ca parākramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Pauruṣa, vikrama, śaurya, śauṭīrya, and parākrama denote valor or heroic energy.
The might born from treasury and army is prabhāva; one who has it is pratāpavat.

children.text: bhiyā dharmārthakāmaiśca parīkṣā yā tu sopadhā ||
children.translated_text: A test made through fear, dharma, wealth, and desire is called sopadhā.
Counsel and related matters are not to have six eyes; they are outside the reach of a third person or more.
Mantra means secret deliberation; rahas, channa, and upahvara mean hidden or secret.
Vivikta, vijana, ekānta, niḥśalāka, and kevala mean secluded, solitary, or alone.
Rahasya is used in the sense of a secret; nyāya means what is fitting, proper, or well ordered.
Naya means policy or right conduct; nyāyya, ucita, yukta, and sāmprata mean proper or suitable.
Labhya, prāpta, bhajamāna, abhinīta, and upayika mean obtainable, attained, or appropriate.
Prakriyā means procedure or authority; maryādā, dhāraṇā, and sthiti denote a rule, limit, or established order.
Saṃsthā means an established arrangement; aparādha, mantu, vyalīka, vipriya, and āgas denote an offence.

children.text: baliḥ karo bhāgadheyo dvipādyo dviguṇo damaḥ
children.translated_text: Bali, kara, and bhāgadheya denote tax or tribute; dvipādya or dviguṇa is a double fine, and dama is a penalty.
Vāhinī, pṛtanā, senā, bala, sainya, and anīkinī mean army.
Kaṭaka, dhvajinī, tantra, daṇḍa, anīka, and patākinī are also words for an army.
Varūthinī, camū, and cakra likewise mean an army; its station is a skandhāvāra, an encampment.

children.text: śibiraṃ racanā tu syādvyūho daṇḍādiko yudhi
children.translated_text: Śibira means camp; racanā or vyūha means a battle formation, such as the daṇḍa formation.
Pratyāsāra, vyūhapārṣṇi, and pratigraha denote the rear of a formation or the back of an army.
A patti consists of one elephant, one chariot, three horses, and five foot soldiers.

children.text: senā senāmukhaṃ gulmo vāhinī pṛtānā camūḥ ||
children.translated_text: Senā, senāmukha, gulma, vāhinī, pṛtanā, camū,
and anīkinī are formed in sequence by tripling the elephants and other members of a patti.
Ten anīkinīs make an akṣauhiṇī; sajjana means equipment, readiness, or protective preparation.

children.text: vaijayantī punaḥ ketuḥ patākā ketanaṃ dhvajaḥ
children.translated_text: Vaijayantī, ketu, patākā, ketana, and dhvaja mean a banner or flag.
Its two tufts or fringes are called uccūla and avacūla, upward-facing and downward-facing tassels.

children.text: gajo vājī rathaḥ pattiḥ senāṅgaṃ syāccaturvidham
children.translated_text: Elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry are the four divisions of an army.
For war, a wheeled vehicle is a ratha, also called śatāṅga or syandana.
A chariot for play is called puṣparatha, while one intended for divine use is marudratha.
A serviceable chariot is yogya-ratha; vainayika, adhvaratha, and pariyānika are further chariot terms.
Karṇīratha, pravahaṇa, ḍayana, and rathagarbhaka are names of carriage-like vehicles.
Anas and śakaṭa denote a cart; gantrī and kambalibāhyaka are also cart or wagon terms.
Next, when a chariot is covered with blankets, cloths, and the like, it receives corresponding names such as kāmbala and vāstra.
The one covered with pale or white blankets is called pāṇḍukambalī.

children.text: sa tu dvaipo vaiyāghraśca yo vṛto dvipicarmaṇā
children.translated_text: That which is covered with leopard or tiger skin is called dvaipa or vaiyāghra.

children.text: rathāṅgaṃ rathapādo 'ri cakraṃ dhārā punaḥ pradhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Rathāṅga, rathapāda, ari, and cakra are words for the wheel; dhārā and pradhi denote the rim.
Nemi is the felly; aṇi and āṇī are the peg at the end of the axle, while nābhi and piṇḍikā denote the hub.
Yugaṃdhara and kūvara name the yoke-bearing pole; yuga is the cross-piece that binds the shaft-ends.
The yoke-pin is called śamyā, and prāsaṅga denotes the space or part at the end of the yoke.

children.text: anukarṣo dārvadhaḥsthaṃ dhurvī yānamukhaṃ ca dhūḥ ||
children.translated_text: Anukarṣa is the lower wooden piece; dhurvī and dhūḥ denote the front or pole of a vehicle.
Rathagupti is the varūtha, the protective covering of a chariot, and apaskara denotes the chariot fittings.
A śibikā is a borne conveyance; dolā and preṅkhā and related words denote a swing or suspended carriage.
Vainītaka denotes mutual carrying, such as transport by a palanquin and the like.

children.text: yānaṃ yugyaṃ pattraṃ vāhyaṃ vahyaṃ vāhanadhoraṇe ||
children.translated_text: Yāna, yugya, pattra, vāhya, and vahya are vehicle terms in the sense of a conveyance or draught-carriage.
Niyantṛ, prājitṛ, yantṛ, sūta, savyeṣṭhṛ, and sārathī are names for a driver or charioteer.
Dakṣiṇastha, pracetā, kṣattṛ, and rathakuṭumbika are likewise terms for the chariot attendant or driver.

children.text: rathārohiṇi tu rathī rathike rathiro rathī
children.translated_text: For one mounted in a chariot, the terms are rathin, rathika, rathira, and rathī.

children.text: aśvārohe tvaśvavāraḥ sādī ca turagī ca saḥ ||
children.translated_text: For a horse-rider, the terms are aśvavāra, sādī, and turagī.
For one mounted on an elephant, sādī, yantṛ, mahāmātra, and niṣādin are used.
Ādhoraṇa, hastipaka, gajājīva, and ibhapālaka are elephant-driver or elephant-keeper terms.
Yoddhṛ, bhaṭa, and yodha are fighters; senārakṣa and sainika are soldiers guarding the army.

children.text: senāyāṃ ye samavetāste sainyāḥ sainikā api ||
children.translated_text: Those who are gathered in an army are called sainya and also sainika.
Those who fight by the thousand are called sāhasra and sahasrin.
Chāyākara and chatradhāra name an umbrella-bearer; patākin and vaijayantika name a banner-bearer.
Paridhistha means a circumstanding attendant, and paricara a servant; āmukta means put on or attached, like pratimukta.
Apinaddha and pinaddha mean fastened; saṃnaddha and vyūḍhakaṅkaṭa mean armed or clad in armor.

children.text: daṃśito varmitaḥ sajjaḥ saṃnāho varma kaṅkaṭaḥ
children.translated_text: Daṃśita, varmita, and sajja mean equipped with armor; saṃnāha, varman, and kaṅkaṭa are armor.
Jagara, kavaca, daṃśa, tanutra, māṭhya, and uraśchada are terms for a cuirass or breast-armor.
Nicolaka, kūrpāsa, vāravāṇa, and kañcuka name a coat, jacket, or corselet.
Sārasana is an additional piece worn on the chest together with corselets.

children.text: śirastrāṇe tu śīrṣaṇyaṃ śiraskaṃ śīrṣakaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: For a helmet or head-protector, the words are śīrṣaṇya, śiraska, and śīrṣaka.
Nāgoda denotes protection for the belly, while matkuṇa denotes protection for the shins or legs.
Bāhula is an arm-guard, and jālikā is a bodily protector.
A jālikā may be an iron mail-like covering; āyudhīya denotes one who lives by weapons.
Kāṇḍapṛṣṭha and āyudhika are equivalent weapon-man terms, as prāsika and kauntika are spear-bearer terms.
Pāraśvadhika, pāraśvadha, and paraśvadhāyudha denote a man armed with an axe.
Naistriṃśika, śāktīka, and yāṣṭīka are men bearing those respective weapons, a sword, spear, and staff.
Tūṇin is a quiver-bearer; dhanurbhṛt and dhānuṣka denote an archer, while kāṇḍīra means one who has arrows.
Kṛtahasta and kṛtapuṅkha denote one whose arrows are well applied and well shot.
Śīghravedhin and laghuhasta mean a quick shooter; for a missed arrow the text gives lakṣyataḥ.
Cyuteṣu denotes one whose arrow has slipped or failed; dūravedhin is one who shoots far, and durāpālya is a weapon hard to ward off.
Heti, praharaṇa, śastra, and astra are weapons, and that category is fourfold.
A released weapon is of two kinds, hand-released and mechanism-released, such as a spear or arrow.
An unreleased weapon is a knife and the like; a staff and similar weapons have a double nature.
Dhanuṣ, cāpa, astra, iṣvāsa, kodaṇḍa, dhanvan, and kārmuka are words for a bow.
Druṇa and lastaka denote the bow-stave; its inner end is also called arti or aṭanī.

children.text: maurvī jīvā guṇo gavyā śiñjā bāṇāsanaṃ druṇā
children.translated_text: Maurvī, jīvā, guṇa, gavyā, and śiñjā are names for the bowstring; bāṇāsana and druṇā also belong to bow terminology.

children.text: śiñjinī jyā ca godhā tu talaṃ jyāghātavāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Śiñjinī and jyā are also bowstrings; godhā and tala are guards against the blow of the bowstring.
Ālīḍha, vaiśākha, pratyālīḍha, and maṇḍala are shooting stances,

children.text: samapādaṃ ca vedhyaṃ tu lakṣyaṃ lakṣaṃ śaravyakam ||
children.translated_text: and samapāda as well; the target to be pierced is lakṣya, lakṣa, or śaravyaka.
For an arrow there are the terms pṛṣatka, viśikha, khaga, gārdhrapakṣa, kāṇḍa, āśuga, pradara, sāyaka, and patravāha,
as well as patrī, iṣu, ajihmaga, śilīmukha, kaṅkapatra, ropa, kalamba, śara, mārgaṇa, and citrapuṅkha.
Prakṣveḍana, sarvaloha, nārāca, and eṣaṇa name an all-iron arrow.
A sent arrow is nirasta or prahita; one smeared with poison is viṣākta, digdha, or liptaka.
Bāṇamukti and vyavaccheda mean the release of an arrow; dīpti is the sharp intensity of its speed.
Kṣurapra, tadbala, ardhendu, tīra-mukha, and the like are varieties of it.

children.text: pakṣo vāja: pattraṇā tannyāsaḥ puṅkhastu kartarī
children.translated_text: Pakṣa, vāja, and pattraṇa are the feathers; their setting is tannyāsa, while puṅkha is the rear fletching, also called kartarī.
Tūṇa, niṣaṅga, tūṇīra, upāsaṅga, and śarāśraya are names for a quiver.
Śaradhi and kalāpa are also quiver terms; next candrahāsa, karavāla, nistriṃśa, kṛpāṇa, and khaḍga are sword terms.
Taravāri, kaukṣeyaka, maṇḍalāgra, asi, ṛṣṭi, and riṣṭi are also sword terms; its hilt is tsaru or muṣṭi.
Pratyākāra, parīvāra, and kośa denote the scabbard, the covering of a sword.
Aṅkana, phalaka, carma, kheṭaka, āvaraṇa, and sphara are shield terms.

children.text: asya muṣṭistu saṃgrāhaḥ kṣurī churī kṛpāṇikā
children.translated_text: Its grip is called saṃgrāha; kṣurī, churī, and kṛpāṇikā are knife terms.
Śastrī and asidhenuputrī are further knife names; patrapāla and sāyatā are transmitted here as related terms.
Daṇḍa, yaṣṭi, and laguḍa are staff or club terms; īlī and karavālikā are listed next.

children.text: bhindipāle sṛgaḥ kunte prāso 'tha drughaṇo ghanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the bhindipāla the term is sṛga; kunta and prāsa denote a lance, while drughaṇa and ghana denote a mallet.
Mudgara is a mace or hammer; kuṭhāra, paraśu, parśu, and parśvadha are axe terms.
Paraśvadha and svadhiti are also axe terms; parigha and parighātana denote an iron bar or bludgeon.
Sarvalā and tomara are javelin terms; śalya is a point, śaṅku a spike, and śūla or triśīrṣaka a spear or trident-like weapon.
Śakti, paṭṭiśa, duḥsphoṭa, cakra, and the like are classes of weapons.
Khuralī denotes exertion or drill; yogyābhyāsa is the training of a draught animal, and the ground for it is khalūrikā.
Sarvābhisāra, sarvaugha, and sarvasaṃhanana are equivalent terms for a general mustering.
Lohābhisāra is the rite on the tenth day, after the nīrājana ceremony.
Prasthāna, gamana, vrajyā, abhiniryāṇa, and prayāṇaka mean departure or setting out.
Yātrā and abhiṣeṇana mean going against an enemy with an army.
Āsāra is the force of an ally; pracakra is an army that has set itself in motion.
Prasāra, or prasaraṇa, is an expedition for the sake of grass, wood, and the like.
Abhikrama is the movement in battle of a fearless man toward his enemies.
Abhyamitrya, abhyamitrīya, and abhyamitrīṇa denote one who is going against the enemy.
Usvānu and rasila are terms for the vigorous; urjasvin and urjasvala are equivalent.
Sāṃyugīna means skilled in battle; jetṛ, jiṣṇu, and jitvara mean a conqueror.

children.text: jayyo yaḥ śakyate jetuṃ jeyo jetavyamātrake ||
children.translated_text: Jayya is one who can be conquered; jeya is simply one who is to be conquered.
Vaitālika, bodhakara, arthika, and saukhasuptika are terms for awakeners or panegyrists.
Ghāṇṭika, cākrika, sūta, bandin, and maṅgalapāṭhaka are also bards or auspicious reciters.
Māgadha and magadha denote a bard; saṃśaptakas are those who do not turn back from battle.
Nagna is one whose vow is praise; his text is called Bhogāvalī.

children.text: prāṇaḥ sthāma taraḥ parākramabaladyumnāni śauryaujasī śuṣmaṃ śuṣma ca śaktirūrjasahasī yuddhaṃ tu saṃkhyaṃ kaliḥ
children.translated_text: Prāṇa, sthāman, taras, parākrama, bala, dyumna, śaurya, ojas, śuṣma or śuṣman, śakti, ūrj, and sahas denote strength or martial power; yuddha is also called saṃkhya and kali.

children.text: saṃgrāmāhavasaṃprahārasamarā janyaṃ yudāyodhanaṃ saṃsphoṭaḥ kalaho mṛdhaṃ praharaṇaṃ saṃyadraṇo vigrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Saṃgrāma, āhava, saṃprahāra, samara, janya, yudh, āyodhana, saṃsphoṭa, kalaha, mṛdha, praharaṇa, saṃyad, raṇa, and vigraha are terms for battle.
Dvandva, samāghāta, samāhvaya, abhisaṃpāta, saṃmarda, samit, and praghāta are further terms for conflict.
Āskandana, āji, pradhana, anīka, abhyāgama, and pravidāraṇa are also battle terms.
Samudāya, samudaya, rāṭi, samiti, and saṃgara are terms for an encounter or battle-array.
Abhyāmarda, saṃparāya, samīka, and sāṃparāyika also denote battle or close combat.
Ākranda and saṃyuga are battle terms; niyuddha is the combat that arises from the arms, that is, hand-to-hand fighting.
Paṭaha and āḍambara are equivalent terms for martial din; tumula means confused and crowded with battle.
Nāsīra is the front march or vanguard; avamarda means crushing or pressure.
Prapāta is an assault; abhyavaskanda, dhāṭī, and abhyāsādana have the same sense.
When such an attack occurs at night it is sauptika; vīrāśaṃsana denotes a battlefield, a place terrible in combat.
Niyuddhabhū and akṣavāṭa name a wrestling ground; moha, mūrchā, and kaśmala mean stupor or fainting.

children.text: vṛtte bhāvini vā yuddhe pānaṃ syādvīrapāṇakam
children.translated_text: When battle has taken place or is still to come, the drinking is called vīrapāṇaka, the warriors' drink.
Palāyana, apayāna, saṃdāva, drava, and vidrava are terms for flight.
Apakrama and drāva also denote retreat; vijaya and jaya mean victory.
Parājaya and bhaṅga mean defeat in battle; ḍamara, ḍimba, and viplava denote disorder or revolt.
Vairaniryātana, vairaśuddhi, and vairapratikriyā mean the requital or clearing of enmity.
Balātkāra, prasabha, and haṭha mean force or violence; skhalita and chala mean a slip or deceit.
Parāparyabhita, bhūta, jita, bhagna, and parājita mean conquered or defeated.
Palāyita means fled: one who is lost, has taken to a direction, or has disappeared.
Jitāhava and jitakāśin mean victorious in battle; praskanna and patita are equivalent, meaning fallen.

children.text: cāraḥ kārā guptau vandyāṃ grahakaḥ prāpato grahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Cāra and kāra belong to guarding or spying; in captivity, grahaka, prāpata, and graha denote seizer or seizure.
Cāturvarṇya, the fourfold varṇa order, is the division of men into dvija, kṣatra, vaiśya, and śūdra.
In order, the four āśramas are brahmacārin, gṛhin, vānaprastha, and bhikṣu.
There are four āśramas; among them varṇin denotes the brahmacārin.
Jyeṣṭhāśramin, gṛhamedhin, gṛhastha, snātaka, and gṛhin are terms for a householder.
Vaikhānasa and vānaprastha denote a forest hermit; bhikṣu, sāṃnyāsika, and yati denote a renunciant.
Karmandin and raktavasana are ascetic terms, as are parivrājaka and tāpasa.
Pārāśarī, pārikāṅkṣī, maskarī, and pārirakṣaka are names of ascetic types.
Sthāṇḍila, or sthaṇḍilaśāyin, is one who, by vow, sleeps on the bare ground.
One who endures the hardships of austerity is dānta, śānta, śrānta, or jitendriya, self-controlled.
Avadāna is pure action; a brāhmaṇa is called trayīmukha, one whose mouth is the three Vedas.
Bhūdeva, vāḍava, and vipra are terms for a brāhmaṇa; jātija and janmaja refer to one born by birth.
Varṇajyeṣṭha, sūtrakaṇṭha, ṣaṭkarman, and mukhasaṃbhava are further terms for a brāhmaṇa.

children.text: vedagarbhaḥ śamīgarbhaḥ sāvitro maittra eva saḥ
children.translated_text: He is also called vedagarbha, śamīgarbha, sāvitra, and maitra.
Baṭu and māṇavaka mean a young student; bhikṣā is a mere morsel of begged food.
Upanāya, upanaya, baṭūkaraṇa, and ānaya are terms for initiation as a student.
Agnīndhana and agnikārya denote the tending of the sacred fire; agnīdhra and agnikārikā are related fire-service terms.

children.text: pālāśo daṇḍa āṣāḍho vrate rāmbhastu vaiṇavaḥ
children.translated_text: Pālāśa and āṣāḍha are staff names; in a vow, rāmbha is the same as vaiṇava.
Bailva, sārasvata, raucya, pailava, and auparodhika are further names for ritual staffs or observance-types.
Āśvattha, jitanemi, audumbara, and ulūkhala are also listed among these terms.

children.text: jaṭā saṭā vṛṣī pīṭhaṃ kuṇḍikā tu kamaṇḍaluḥ ||
children.translated_text: Jaṭā and saṭā mean matted hair; vṛṣī and pīṭha mean a seat; kuṇḍikā and kamaṇḍalu mean a water-pot.
Śrotriya and chāndasa denote one learned in the Veda; yaṣṭṛ and anvādeṣṭṛ are sacrificer terms, and vratin is used in a sacrifice.
Yājaka and yajamāna are sacrificial officiant and patron terms; a somayājī is one who is consecrated.
Ijyāśīla, yāyajūka, yajvan, and āsutībala denote one devoted to sacrificing.
Somapa and somapīthin mean a Soma-drinker; sthapati, gīḥpati, and iṣṭikṛt are ritual titles.
Sarvavedas denotes one who has performed a sacrifice with all his property as the sacrificial fee.
The knower of the <s>Yajurveda</s> is the adhvaryu; the knower of the <s>Ṛgveda</s> is the hotṛ; the udgātṛ is the knower of the <s>Sāmaveda</s>.

children.text: yajño yāgaḥ savaḥ sattraṃ stomo manyurmakhaḥ kratuḥ
children.translated_text: Yajña, yāga, sava, sattra, stoma, manyu, makha, and kratu are words for sacrifice.
Saṃstara, saptatantu, vitāna, barhis, and adhvara also belong to the vocabulary of sacrifice.
Study is brahmayajña; an oblation is devayajña.
Homa, hotra, and vaṣaṭkāra are offering terms; pitṛyajña is tarpaṇa, libation to the ancestors.
That is also śrāddha and piṇḍadāna; nṛyajña is honoring a guest.
Bhūtayajña is bali, an offering to beings; these are the five mahāyajñas.
Paurṇamāsa and darśa are two separate sacrifices at the ends of the fortnights.
The saumikī iṣṭi is the dīkṣiṇīya rite; dīkṣā is the undertaking of vows.

children.text: vṛttiḥ sugahanā kumbā vedī bhūmiḥ pariṣkṛtā
children.translated_text: Vṛtti, sugahanā, and kumbā are altar terms; the vedī is prepared ground.
Sthaṇḍila and catvara are other altar grounds; the yūpa is the sacrificial post.
Caṣāla, yūpakaṭaka, and yūpakarṇa denote the ghee-smeared upper fitting of a sacrificial post.
Araṇi is the wood used for producing fire by churning, at the upper part of the sacrificial post.
The three fires are the dakṣiṇa, the āhavanīya, and the gārhapatya.
This triad of fires is called tretā; a fire that has been brought forward and ritually prepared is praṇīta or saṃskṛta.
The ṛc by which kindling is laid on is called sāmidhenī and also dhāyyā.
Samidh, indhana, medha, idhma, tarpaṇa, and edhas are words for fuel; ash is called the following.
Ash is bhūti, bhasita, rakṣā, and kṣāra; a ritual vessel is a pātra, such as a sruva and the like.
Sruva, sruc, adharā, upabhṛt, and juhū are ladles; the juhū is again the upper one.
The dhruvā is the general name for the vessel in which clarified butter is placed.
An animal that is consecrated by mantra and then slain is called an upākṛta paśu.

children.text: paramparākaṃ śasanaṃ prokṣaṇaṃ ca vadho makhe
children.translated_text: In a sacrifice, killing is called paramparāka, śasana, and prokṣaṇa.
A rite intended to harm is abhichāra; what is fit for sacrifice is yajñiya.
Havis, sāṃnāyya, and āmikṣā denote curd formed in boiled warm milk.

children.text: kṣīraśaraḥ payasyā ca tanmastuni tu vājinam ||
children.translated_text: Kṣīraśara and payasyā are terms for that milk preparation; the watery part in it is vājinam.
What is to be given to the gods is havya; what is for the ancestors is kavya, namely cooked rice.
Clarified butter mixed with curd is called pṛṣadājya and pṛṣātaka.
Curd mixed with honey is madhuparka, also called mahodaya.
Havitrī is the fire-pit for oblation; havyapāka and caru are cooked offerings.
The remainder of a sacrifice is amṛta; leftover food after eating is vighasa.
The end of a sacrifice is avabhṛtha; pūrta means works such as wells, while iṣṭa is sacrificial action.
Iṣṭāpūrta is the combination of both; barhis is a handful of sacrificial grass, also called viṣṭara.
Agnihotrin, agnivit, and āhitāgni denote one who has established and maintains the sacred fires.
Agnyādhāna and agnihotra relate to the keeping of the fire; a darvī is a spoon for drawing clarified butter.
The offering-fire with great flame is mahājvāla and mahāvīra, as in the pravargya rite.
The smoke of the oblation is nigaṇa; the ash of the oblation is vaiṣṭuta.
Upasparśa is ācamana, ritual sipping; ghāra and seka are sprinkling or pouring.
Brahmāsana is the seat for meditation and yoga; brahmavarcas is sacred brilliance.
Brahmavarcas also means prosperity from conduct and study; in recitation, brahmāñjali is the joined hands.
In recitation, droplets issuing from the mouth are called brahmabindus.
A complete utterance is pārāyaṇa; in ritual procedure, kalpa, vidhi, and krama denote rule and order.
At the base of the thumb is the brāhma tīrtha; at the little finger is the kāya tīrtha.
Between the forefinger and thumb is the pitrya tīrtha; at the tips of the fingers is the daivata tīrtha.
Brahmatva, brahmabhūya, and brahmasāyujya are terms for becoming or union with Brahman.
Devabhūya and similar expressions are to be understood in the same way; upākaraṇa is the formal beginning of Vedic study.
The taking up of the Veda after the preliminary saṃskāra is upākaraṇa; svādhyāya and japa are recitation.
Aupavasta and upavāsa mean fasting; kṛcchra includes observances such as sāṃtapana.
Prāya is the fast unto death of a renouncer; niyama, puṇyaka, and vrata are observances or vows.
Caritra, carita, ācāra, cāritra, and caraṇa are words for conduct.
Vṛtta and śīla are also conduct; aghamarṣaṇa is a japa that destroys all sins.
Pādagrahaṇa, abhivādana, and upasaṃgraha are equivalent terms for respectful salutation.
Upavīta and yajñasūtra denote the sacred thread when the right arm is drawn out.
Prācīnāvīta is when it is worn on the other side; nivīta is when it hangs from the neck.
<s>Prācetasa</s> is <s>Vālmīki</s>, the poet; <s>Valmīka</s> and <s>Kuśina</s> are also his names.
<s>Maitrāvaruṇa</s> and <s>Vālmīka</s> are further names; <s>Vedavyāsa</s> is <s>Māṭhara</s>.
<s>Dvaipāyana</s>, <s>Pārāśarya</s>, <s>Kānīna</s>, and <s>Bādarāyaṇa</s> are names of <s>Vyāsa</s>.
The mother of <s>Vyāsa</s> is <s>Ambā</s>, <s>Satyavatī</s>, <s>Vāsavī</s>, and <s>Gandhakālikā</s>.
She is also <s>Yojanagandhā</s>, <s>Dāśeyī</s>, and the daughter of <s>Śālaṅkāyana</s>.
<s>Jāmadagnya</s> is <s>Rāma</s>, <s>Bhārgava</s>, and the son of <s>Reṇukā</s>.
<s>Nārada</s> is <s>Devabrahmā</s>, <s>Piśuna</s>, and <s>Kalikāraka</s>.
<s>Vasiṣṭha</s> is the husband of <s>Arundhatī</s>; <s>Akṣamālā</s> is <s>Arundhatī</s>.
<s>Triśaṅkuyājī</s> and <s>Gādheya</s> are <s>Viśvāmitra</s>, also called <s>Kauśika</s>.
<s>Kuśāraṇi</s> is <s>Durvāsas</s>; <s>Śatānanda</s> is <s>Gautama</s>.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> is <s>Brahmarātri</s> and <s>Yogeśa</s>; now the names of <s>Pāṇini</s> are given.
<s>Sālāturīya</s> and <s>Dākṣeya</s> are names of <s>Pāṇini</s>; <s>Gonardīya</s> is <s>Patañjali</s>.
<s>Kātyāyana</s> is <s>Vararuci</s>, <s>Medhāji</s>, and <s>Punarvasu</s>.
<s>Vyāḍi</s> is <s>Vindhyavāsī</s>, and he is also <s>Nandinītanaya</s>.
<s>Sphoṭāyana</s> is <s>Kakṣīvat</s>; <s>Pālakāpya</s> is <s>Kareṇubhū</s>.
<s>Vātsyāyana</s> is <s>Mallanāga</s>; <s>Kauṭalya</s> is the son of <s>Caṇaka</s>.
<s>Drāmila</s>, <s>Pakṣilasvāmin</s>, <s>Viṣṇugupta</s>, and <s>Aṅgula</s> are also his names.
Kṣatavrata and avakīrṇin denote one whose vow is broken; a vrātya is one lacking the saṃskāras.
Śiśvidāna and kṛṣṇakarman denote one of dark deeds; brahmabandhu is a base twice-born man.
Naṣṭāgni, vīrahā, jātimātrajīvin, and dvijabruva denote a Brahmin in name only.
Dharmadhvajin and liṅgavṛtti denote a religious hypocrite; vedahīna and nirākṛti denote one without the Veda.

children.text: vārtāśī bhojanārthaṃ yo gotrādi vadati svakam ||
children.translated_text: Vārtāśin is one who states his gotra and the like for the sake of food.
Ucchiṣṭabhojana is one who eats leftovers, divine offerings, and bali portions.
Ajapa is a bad reciter or student; śākhāraṇḍa is one attached to another Vedic branch.
Śastrājīvin and kāṇḍapṛṣṭha denote one who lives by weapons; guruhā and narakalika denote a teacher-killer.
Mala, aśrāddha, and malimluca denote one unfit for worship of gods and similar rites.
One fallen from the five sacrifices is so called; kharu is one whose sole taste is for what is forbidden.
When the sun rises or sets while someone is asleep, the two cases are named in order as follows.
They are abhyudita and abhinirmukta; vīrojjha is one who does not perform the oblation.
Vīropajīvika is one intent on begging under the pretext of maintaining the agnihotra.
Vīraviplāvaka is one who sacrifices with wealth collected from Śūdras.
The proponent of syādvāda is an Ārhata; the proponent of emptiness is a Saugata.
A Naiyāyika is an <s>Akṣapāda</s>; a Yoga follower is yauga, and a Sāṃkhya is Kāpila.
A Vaiśeṣika is Aulūkya; a Bārhaspatya is Nāstika.
A Cārvāka is Laukāyatika; all these six are tārkikas.

children.text: kṣatraṃ tu kṣattriyo rājā rājanyo bāhusaṃbhavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Kṣatra, kṣattriya, rājā, rājanya, and bāhusaṃbhava are terms for a Kshatriya or king.

children.text: aryā bhūmispṛśo vaiśyā ūravyā ūrajā viśaḥ
children.translated_text: Vaiśyas are called ārya, bhūmispṛś, ūravyā, ūraja, and viś.

children.text: vāṇijyaṃ pāśupālyaṃ ca karṣaṇaṃ ceti vṛttayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Their livelihoods are commerce, cattle-keeping, and ploughing or agriculture.
Ājīva, jīvana, vārtā, jīvikā, vṛtti, and vetana are words for livelihood or means of support.
Uñcha is the taking of stray grain kernels; śila is the gathering of ears of grain and the like.
That pair is called ṛta; agriculture is anṛta, while what is obtained by asking is mṛta.
What is received without asking is amṛta; a livelihood by service is called a dog-like livelihood.

children.text: satyānṛtaṃ tu vāṇijyaṃ vaṇijyā vāṇijo vaṇik
children.translated_text: Commerce is called satyānṛta; vaṇijyā, vāṇija, and vaṇik are merchant terms.
Krayavikrayika, paṇyājīva, upaṇika, and naigama are also terms for a trader or merchant.
Vaideha, sārthavāha, kāyaka, krayika, and krayī are further merchant terms.
With the prefix vi- these indicate selling; vasna, ardha, and avakraya are terms for price or value.
Mūladravya and paripaṇa denote capital; nīvī, lābha, adhika, and phala denote profit or gain.
Paridāna, vinimaya, naimeya, and parivartana are terms for exchange or barter.
Vyatihāra, parāvarta, vaimeya, and vimaya are likewise terms for exchange.
Nikṣepa and upanidhi mean a deposit or entrusted property; pratidāna is its return or handing back.

children.text: kretavyamātrake kreyaṃ krayyaṃ nyastaṃ krayāya yat
children.translated_text: Kreya and krayya denote something simply to be bought, something set aside for purchase.

children.text: paṇitavyaṃ tu vikreyaṃ paṇyaṃ satyāpanaṃ punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Vikreya and paṇya denote what is to be sold; satyāpana is an earnest or confirming payment.
Satyaṃkāra and satyākṛti are equivalent to it; vipaṇa and vikraya are equivalent words for sale.

children.text: gaṇyaṃ gaṇeyaṃ saṃkhyeyaṃ saṃkhyā tvekādikā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: Gaṇya, gaṇeya, and saṃkhyeya mean countable; saṃkhyā, number, begins with one and the rest.
Each succeeding number is ten times the previous one, beginning from one and then ten.
The sequence continues as hundred, thousand, ayuta, lakṣa, prayuta, and koṭi.

children.text: arbudamabjaṃ kharvaṃ ca nikharvaṃ ca mahāmbujam
children.translated_text: Then come arbuda, abja, kharva, nikharva, and mahāmbuja.
The names further include śaṅku, vārdhi, antya, madhya, and parārdha.
Asaṃkhya denotes the innumerable; infinities such as those of islands, oceans, matter, and souls are called anantaka.
A sāṃyātrika is a ship-merchant; yānāpātra and vahitraka are words for a vessel.
Vohittha, vahana, and pota are ship terms; potavāha and niyāmaka denote one who guides a ship.
Niyāma and karṇadhāra mean helmsman; nāvika is a sailor, and nau and maṅginī are boat terms.
Tarī, tariṇī, veḍī, and droṇī are also words for a wooden vessel that carries one over water.
A boat-pole or oar is kṣepaṇī; the guṇavṛkṣa, or mast, is called kūpaka.
Polindas are inner cross-beams; maṅga is the head or prow of the maṅginī boat.
Abhri is a wooden spade; sekapātra and secana are terms for a bailing vessel.
Kenipāta and koṭipātra are terms connected with the oar; uḍupa and plava mean a raft or float.
Kola, bhela, and taraṇḍa are raft terms; tarapaṇya is the fare paid for crossing.
A person living by interest is called vṛddhyājīva, dvaiguṇika, vārdhuṣika, or kusīdaka.
Vārdhuṣi and kusīda denote the employment of money for interest, a livelihood based on increase.
Vṛddhi and kalāntara mean interest; ṛṇa, uddhāra, and paryudañcana denote debt or loan.
What is obtained by asking is yācitaka; what is obtained by exchange is āpamityaka.
The adhamarṇa is the receiver or debtor, while the uttamarṇa is the giver or creditor.
Pratibhū and lagnaka mean a surety; sākṣī and stheya denote a witness, and ādhi and bandhaka a pledge.
Pautava is measurement by scales and the like; druvaya is measurement by kuḍava and similar vessels.
Pāyya is measurement by the hand and similar units; in that system five ruñjās make one māṣaka.

children.text: te tu ṣoḍaśa karṣo 'kṣaḥ palaṃ karṣacatuṣṭayam
children.translated_text: Sixteen of those māṣakas make a karṣa or akṣa; four karṣas make a pala.
For gold, an akṣa is called bista or suvarṇa; a kurubista corresponds to that pala measure.

children.text: tulā palaśataṃ tāsāṃ viṃśatyā bhāra ācitaḥ
children.translated_text: A tulā is one hundred palas; by twenty such tulās a bhāra, also called ācita, is made.
Ten ācitas make the measures called śākaṭa, śākaṭīna, and śalāṭa.
Four kuḍavas make a prastha, and four prasthas make an āḍhaka.
Four āḍhakas make a droṇa, and a khārī is made from sixteen droṇas.
A hasta is twenty-four aṅgulas, and a daṇḍa is four hastas.

children.text: tatsahasraṃ tu gavyūtaṃ krośastau dvau tu gorutam ||
children.translated_text: A thousand such daṇḍas make a gavyūta; two gavyūtas make a krośa, also called goruta.
Gavyā, gavyūta, and gavyūti are equivalent terms; four krośas make a yojana.
Pāśupālya and jīvavṛtti denote cattle-keeping; gomān, gomī, and gavīśvara denote an owner or lord of cattle.
Gopāla, goduh, ābhīra, gopa, gosaṃkhya, and ballava are cowherd terms.
Govinda denotes one appointed over cows; jābāla is one whose livelihood depends on goats.
Kuṭumbin, karṣaka, kṣetrin, halin, kṛṣika, and kārṣika are terms for a farmer or cultivator.

children.text: kṛṣīvalo 'pi jityā tu hali: sīrastu lāṅgalam ||
children.translated_text: Kṛṣīvala is also a cultivator; halin is a ploughman, while sīra and lāṅgala are plough terms.
Godāraṇa and hala denote the plough; īṣā and sītā denote its pole and furrow-line.

children.text: nirīṣe kuṭakaṃ phāle kṛṣakaḥ kuśikaḥ phalam ||
children.translated_text: When without an īṣā it is kuṭaka; phāla, kṛṣaka, kuśika, and phala are terms for the ploughshare.

children.text: dātraṃ lavitraṃ tanmuṣṭau vaṇṭo matyaṃ samīkṛtau
children.translated_text: Dātra and lavitra mean a sickle; for its hand-grip the words vaṇṭa and matya are treated as equivalent.
Godāraṇa and kuddāla are hoe or mattock terms; khanitra and avadāraṇa denote a digging implement.
Pratoda, pravayaṇa, prājana, and totra are goad terms, instruments for prodding.
Yotra and yoktra denote a harnessing strap; koṭiśa is an implement for breaking clods.

children.text: medhirmethiḥ khale vālī khale gobandhadāru yat
children.translated_text: Medhi, methi, and vālī are terms for the wooden post in the threshing-floor to which cattle are tied.
Śūdra, antyavarṇa, vṛṣala, padya, pajja, and jaghanyaja are terms for the lowest varṇa.
The mixed castes include groups beginning with mūrdhābhiṣikta and extending to rathakṛt.
Born from a Brahmin father and a Kṣatriya woman is the mūrdhābhiṣikta; from him with a Vaiśya woman, again,
comes the ambaṣṭha, while with a Śūdra woman arise the pāraśava and niṣāda.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya woman comes the māhiṣya; with a Śūdra woman, the ugra.
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra woman comes the karaṇa; from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya woman, the āyogava.
Again, from a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya woman comes the kṣattā; with a Brahmin woman, the cāṇḍāla.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya woman comes the māgadha; with a Brahmin woman, the vaidehika.
The sūta is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brahmin woman; thus there are twelve subdivisions of that class.
Born from a māhiṣya father and a karaṇī woman is the rathakāraka.

children.text: kārustu kārī prakṛtiḥ śilpī śreṇistu tadguṇe ||
children.translated_text: Kāru, kārī, prakṛti, and śilpin are artisan terms; śreṇi denotes a guild characterized by such a craft.

children.text: śilpaṃ kalā vijñānaṃ ca mālākārastu mālikaḥ
children.translated_text: Śilpa, kalā, and vijñāna mean art or craft; a garland-maker is mālākāra or mālika.
Puṣpājīvin, puṣpalāvin, and avacāyinī denote one who lives by flowers or gathers them.
Kalpapāla, surājīvin, śauṇḍika, and maṇḍahāraka are terms for a liquor seller or one who lives by liquor.
Vārivāsa, pānavaṇij, dhvaja, dhvajin, and āsutībala denote a seller or keeper of drink.

children.text: madyaṃ madiṣṭhā madirā parisrutā kaśyaṃ parisrunmadhu kāpiśāyanam
children.translated_text: Madya, madiṣṭhā, madirā, parisrutā, kaśya, parisrunmadhu, and kāpiśāyana are words for intoxicating liquor.

children.text: gandhottamā kalpamirā pariplutā kādambarī svādurasā halipriyā ||
children.translated_text: Gandhottamā, kalpamirā, pariplutā, kādambarī, svādurasā, and halipriyā are also names for liquor.
Śuṇḍā, hālā, hārahūra, prasannā, vāruṇī, and surā likewise denote liquor.
Mārdvīka, madanā, devasṛṣṭā, kāpiśa, and abdhijā are further liquor terms.
Mādhavaka denotes madhvāsava, mead; śīdhu and āsava denote maireya, a fermented drink.

children.text: jagalo medako malapaṅkaḥ kiṇvaṃ tu nagnahūḥ ||
children.translated_text: Jagala, medaka, and malapaṅka denote the lees; kiṇva is the ferment, also called nagnahū.
Nagnahū and madyabīja mean the seed-ferment of liquor; madyasaṃdhāna and āsuti mean the preparation or fermentation of liquor.
Āsava and abhiṣava are brewing or fermentation; madyamaṇḍa and kārottama are equivalent names for the liquor-scum or sediment.
Galvarka is a caṣaka, a drinking cup; saraka and anuratarṣaṇa are also drinking vessels.
Śuṇḍāpāna, madasthāna, madhuvārā, and madhukrama are terms for a tavern or place of drinking.
Sapīti and sahapāna mean drinking together; āpāna is a drinking assembly, a pānagoṣṭhikā.
Upadaṃśa and avadaṃśa denote a relish eaten with drink; cakṣaṇa is food taken along with liquor.
Nāḍiṃdhama, svarṇakāra, kalāda, and muṣṭika all denote a goldsmith.
Taijasāvartanī and mūṣā are crucibles; bhastrā is a leather bellows.
Āsphoṭinī and vedhanikā are piercing tools; śāṇa, nikaṣa, and kaṣa are whetstone or touchstone terms.

children.text: saṃdaṃśaḥ syātkaṅkamukho bhramaḥ kundaṃ ca yantrakam ||
children.translated_text: Saṃdaṃśa, also called kaṅkamukha, is a pair of tongs; bhrama, kunda, and yantraka name workshop devices or implements.
Vaikaṭika and maṇikāra denote a jeweller; śaulvika denotes a copper-beater.
Śāṅkhika and kāmbavika denote a shell-worker; tunnavāya and saucika denote a tailor or needle-worker.

children.text: kṛpāṇī kartarī kalpanyapi sūcī tu sevanī
children.translated_text: Kṛpāṇī, kartarī, and kalpanī are cutting instruments or scissors; sūcī is a needle, also called sevanī.
Sūcīsūtra is needle-thread, called pippalika; tarku is an implement for working, cutting, or spinning thread.
Piñjana and vihanana denote the bow-like instrument for opening and fluffing cotton.
Sevana, sīvana, and syūti mean sewing; syūta and prasevaka are equivalent terms for something sewn, such as a sewn bag.
Tantuvāya and kuvinda denote a weaver; trasara is a thread-winder or spool.
Vāṇi, vyūti, and vāṇadaṇḍa are loom terms; vemā is a loom, and sūtrāṇi are threads, tantavaḥ.
Nirṇejaka is a washerman, a rajaka; pādukākṛt and carmakṛt denote a shoemaker or leather-worker.
Upānat, pādukā, pādu, pannaddhā, and pādarakṣaṇa are words for footwear.
Prāṇahitā and anupadīnā are footwear terms; what is tied onto the foot is called ābaddhānupada.
Nadhrī, vadhrī, and varatrā denote a strap or thong; ārā is an awl that pierces leather.
Kulāla, kumbhakāra, daṇḍabhṛt, and cakrajīvaka are names for a potter.
Śāṇājīva, śastramārja, bhramāsakta, and asidhāvaka denote a sword-polisher or grinder.
Dhūsara and cākrika denote an oilman or oil-presser; piṇyāka and khala are equivalent terms for oil-cake.
Rathakṛt, sthapati, tvaṣṭṛ, kāṣṭhatakṣan, and vardhakī denote a carpenter or woodworker.
Grāmāyatta and grāmatakṣa denote a village carpenter; kauṭatakṣa and anadhīnaka denote an independent carpenter.
Vṛkṣabhid, takṣaṇī, and vāsī are wood-cutting tools; krakaca and karapattraka denote a saw.

children.text: sa udghano yatra kāṣṭhe kāṣṭhaṃ nikṣipya takṣyate
children.translated_text: The support on which one places wood upon wood and hews it is called an udghana.
Vṛkṣādana and vṛkṣabhedin denote a tree-splitting tool; ṭaṅka is a stone-splitting chisel.
Vyokāra, karmāra, and lohakāra denote a smith; kūṭa is an iron hammer, an ayoghana.
Vraścana and pattraparaśu denote a cutting axe; īṣīkā, tūlikā, and iṣikā are brush or reed terms.
Bhakṣyakāra and kāndavika denote a maker of edible preparations or sweets; kandu and svedanikā are equivalent cooking or steaming vessels.
Raṅgājīva and taulakika denote a dyer; citrakṛt denotes a painter, and then tūlikā is introduced.
Tūlikā is a kūcikā, a brush; citra and ālekhya mean a painting, while palagaṇḍa is a maker of plaster or stucco work.
Pusta is work in plaster and similar materials; nāpita, caṇḍila, and kṣurin denote a barber.
Kṣuramardin, divākīrti, muṇḍaka, and antāvasāyin are also barber terms.
Muṇḍana, bhadrākaraṇa, vapana, and parivāpana mean shaving or tonsure.
Kṣaura is shaving; nārācī denotes a probe or tweezer, an eṣaṇī; devājīva and devala denote one who lives by temple service.
Mārdaṅgika and maurajika denote drum-players; a vīṇā-player is a vaiṇika.
Veṇudhma and vaiṇavika denote a flute-player; pāṇigha and pāṇivādaka denote a hand-percussion player.
Prātihārika and māyājīvin denote a conjurer or illusionist; māyā is called śāmbarī.
Indrajāla, kuhaka, jāla, and kusṛti are terms for magic or trickery.

children.text: kautūhalaṃ tu kutukaṃ kautukaṃ ca kutūhalam ||
children.translated_text: Kautūhala, kutuka, kautuka, and kutūhala mean curiosity, wonder, or amusement.
Vyādha is one who lives by killing animals; lubdhaka and mṛgayu also denote that hunter.
Pāparddhi, mṛgayā, and ākheṭa mean hunting; mṛgavyā and chodana also denote the pursuit or driving of game.
Jālika and vāgurika denote a netter or trapper; vāgurā is an animal-net.

children.text: śumbaṃ varāṭako rajjuḥ śulvaṃ tantrī vaṭī guṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Śumba, varāṭaka, rajju, śulva, tantrī, vaṭī, and guṇa are words for cord, rope, or string.
Dāśa and kaivarta denote a fisherman, a dhīvara; baḍiśa is a fish-hook, an instrument for piercing fish.
Ānāya is a fishing net; kuveṇī is a device for catching fish.
Jīvāntaka and śākunika denote a bird-catcher; vaitaṃsika and saunika denote a trapper or butcher.

children.text: māṃsikaḥ kauṭikaścātha sūnā sthānaṃ vadhasya yat ||
children.translated_text: Māṃsika and kauṭika are butcher terms; sūnā is the place where slaughter takes place.
Vītaṃsa is an apparatus for binding or catching animals and birds.
Pāśa is a binding noose; avapāta and avaṭa are equivalent terms for a pitfall.
Unmātha is a concealed trapping device, a kūṭayantra; vivarṇa denotes a pṛthagjana, an ordinary or socially separate person.

children.text: itaraḥ prākṛto nīcaḥ pāmaro barbaraśca saḥ ||
children.translated_text: Itara, prākṛta, nīca, pāmara, and barbarā also denote such a common or low-status person.
For a caṇḍāla the terms are antāvasāyin, antevāsin, śvapaca, and pukkasa.
Niṣāda, plava, mātaṅga, divākīrti, and janaṃgama are also listed as such outcaste terms.
Pulinda, nāhala, niṣṭya, śabara, āvaruṭa, and bhaṭa are further names in this set.
Māla, bhilla, and kirāta too are all classes called mleccha, non-Vedic or foreign peoples.
